items.title: Captain martyred, 7 terrorists killed in intelligence-based operation in Hangu: ISPR
items.description: The military media affairs wing said on Saturday that a captain was martyred while seven terrorists were killed during an intelligence-based operation (IBO) in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Hangu district. In a statement, Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said security forces conducted an IBO in Hangu on Friday following reports about the presence of terrorists belonging to Fitna al Khawarij — a term the state uses for terrorists belonging to the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan. During the operation, troops effectively engaged the terrorists, it said. “In desperation, the khawarij took refuge inside a mosque, blatantly disregarding the sanctity of the place of worship. In ensuing fire exchange, seven khawarij , belonging to Indian-sponsored Fitna al Khawarij were sent to hell,” it said. The statement went on to say that during the exchange of fire, 27-year-old Captain Hamza Akram, a resident of Punjab’s Narowal district who was “leading his troops from front and relentlessly pursuing” the terrorists, embraced martyrdom. “Weapons and ammunition were also recovered from the killed khawarij , who remained actively involved in numerous terrorist activities against the security forces and law enforcement agencies as well as killing of innocent civilians,” it said. ISPR said that a sanitisation operation was being conducted to eliminate any other Indian-sponsored terrorists in the area. Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi paid tribute to the martyred captain and offered his condolences to the bereaved family. He said that the martyred officer had paid the ultimate sacrifice for the homeland and would remain alive in our hearts. A day earlier, ISPR said 10 terrorists were killed in two separate engagements in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. It said that in the first encounter, a group of terrorists attempted to attack security forces’ checkposts in Azam Warsak area in South Waziristan, which was effectively thwarted, resulting in the deaths of eight terrorists. “In another encounter that took place in Dir district, own troops successfully neutralised two more khawarij ,” it added. Terrorist commander killed in Bannu Separately, security forces killed a key terrorist commander, identified as Jamidullah, during an operation in Jani Khel area of KP’s Bannu district, a security official said. The official said that the terrorist commander was involved in terrorist activities and was considered a quadcopter expert. The official said that security forces conducted the operation in Jani Khel on the basis of intelligence reports, during which Jamidullah was targeted and killed. According to the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies , an Islamabad-based think tank, violence linked to terrorist attacks and counter-terrorism operations intensified sharply in July, making it the deadliest month of 2026, with 112 security personnel among 205 people killed.

items.title: Before AI hits the grid
items.description: PAKISTAN’S announcement that it would allocate 2,000 megawatts of electricity for Bitcoin mining and AI data centres has triggered a predictable debate: can the country afford to supply that much power? It is an important question, but not the most useful one. Bitcoin mining, AI training and real-time digital services do not exactly place identical demands on the electricity system. Pakistan’s electricity challenge is about more than the amount of generation capacity available. It is about when and where electricity is needed, whether the network can deliver it reliably, and how that demand is managed during periods of stress. During the hottest months, cooling demand pushes the grid towards its limits. At other times, generation capacity remains underused. But nationally available capacity does not automatically translate into reliable electricity at the location and hour a data centre requires it. Transmission constraints, substation capacity and power quality matter just as much as the headline allocation. The better question is this: how should this new demand be designed and integrated into the electricity system from the outset? Data centres are not ordinary consumers. Their location, cooling systems, computing equipment and grid connections are decided before construction begins. That gives Pakistan a rare opportunity to shape a major new category of demand before it becomes embedded in the system. But doing so requires recognising that not all computing demand is the same. Some services are highly sensitive to delay. User-facing AI applications, financial platforms and communications systems may require continuous availability. Their loads cannot simply be switched off whenever the grid comes under pressure. Other workloads may offer more flexibility. Certain forms of data processing and model training can be scheduled within broader time windows, distributed across locations or paused at planned checkpoints, depending on how the systems are designed. Pakistan’s electricity challenge is about more than the amount of generation capacity available. Where genuine flexibility exists, it can be reflected in tariffs and connection agreements. Eligible workloads could be scheduled outside critical peak hours. Operators could provide more accurate demand forecasts, limit abrupt changes in consumption, or use storage to reduce pressure on the network during short periods of stress. This is not a hypothetical mechanism. The UN referred to Ireland as a “cautionary tale” when the country faced a severe energy crisis because data centres consume roughly 23 per cent of the nation’s total electricity — nearly rivalling the power used by all residential homes combined. Ireland’s grid operator now assesses new data centre connections in constrained areas partly on whether the applicant can prove its demand is flexible, and writes that commitment directly into the connection agreement rather than leaving it voluntary. Pakistan can build the same discipline in from the start, instead of retrofitting it once the grid is already under strain, the way Ireland had to. Pakistan does not need to begin from scratch. The country already has a cloud-governance and accreditation framework. The Cloud Office is mandated to set standards and compliance requirements for cloud service providers, while the existing accreditation criteria cover security, service availability, resilient power infrastructure and recognised data centre certification. What the framework does not yet fully address is how efficiently these facilities use electricity and water, or how they interact with the wider power system. The Ministry of IT & Telecom’s own concept note identifies this gap. It notes that the current framework does not explicitly prescribe standards for energy management, environmental performance, power usage effectiveness, water usage effectiveness or renewable energy integration. It proposes a national sustainability framework for data centres to fill that gap. That is the right direction. But the framework should go one step further by connecting digital-infrastructure planning with power sector planning. Large facilities should provide credible forecasts of their electricity and water demand. Projects should be assessed against local network capacity, not simply national generation figures. Energy and water performance should be measured consistently. And tariffs should reward verified efficiency and flexibility rather than merely offering cheap electricity to large consumers. This is not anti-investment. Serious data centre investors already consider reliable power, cooling, environmental compliance and long-term energy security when choosing markets. Good standards are not a barrier to investment, but rather, a part of a credible investment proposition. The first generation of AI infrastructure will shape the one that follows. Early decisions on location, efficiency and grid connection will become precedents that are harder to change once major investments have been made. Pakistan does not need to wait for its grid to buckle before it asks this question, the way Ireland did. It has the chance to design demand before it hits the grid, not renegotiate it after the fact. The writer is director, Awareness and Outreach, National Energy Efficiency & Conservation Authority. Published in Dawn, August 8th, 2026

items.title: The supreme sacrifice
items.description: THE police are a vital pillar of our social fabric, serving not only as guardians of the law but also as protectors of the community, said President Asif Ali Zardari on Police Martyrs Day on Aug 4. “Their exemplary courage, firm dedication and ultimate sacrifice in the service of the nation will always inspire pride and command the deepest respect of every citizen of Pakistan,” he added. The prime minister, too, honoured the bravery of police officers who had laid down their lives in the line of duty, noting that the force displays “exceptional professionalism and unflinching resolve” in the nation’s fight against terrorism, violent extremism and crime. The Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies reported that the first seven months of 2026 witnessed 2,786 deaths linked to terrorist violence and counterterrorism operations — 434 security forces’ personnel lost their lives, including 152 police officials in KP and 89 in Balochistan. So far, July has been the deadliest month of 2026, with 112 security officials offering the supreme sacrifice in the line of duty, compared to 38 fatalities a month earlier in June. This is an unprecedented 195 per cent increase in the deaths of law enforcers. At least eight suicide attacks were recorded last month, the highest number in a single month during the past decade. The recent deadly attack near a police station in Swat caused 17 fatalities. As this paper rightly asserted after the Swat bombing, it “is far too high a toll, and the state needs to urgently refine its CT strategy to prevent further loss of precious lives”. Following Police Martyrs Day, one of us convened a forum of serving and retired police officers to discuss the current vulnerabilities and challenges faced by police in general, and those in KP and Balochistan in particular. The trajectory and tenor of violence in these provinces have distinct traits. KP has been on the receiving end since 9/11, paying a huge price in the so-called war against terror. Since Kabul’s takeover by the Taliban in August 2021, violence and bloodshed have assumed greater intensity. Acts of terror have risen exponentially, with fatalities among security forces and civilians progressively rising each year. The last two years have been the worst so far, with police losing 314 personnel. The last two years have been the worst so far, with police losing 314 personnel. Balochistan is facing its fifth (and longest) phase (20 years) of insurgency by separatists. Nawab Akbar Bugti’s killing in a cave near Kohlu in August 2006 was an unfortunate incident that led to a sharp escalation in Baloch militancy. The terrorist nexus of the BLA, BRA and BLF has added lethality to insurgent attacks. BLA’s Majeed Brigade is well-equipped and emulates TTP’s violent tactics. It has superior weaponry, indicating the role of hostile foreign agencies in fomenting unrest in the province. The police’s challenge has increased manifold now that the entire province has been converted into police jurisdiction. The gap in human resources, infrastructure and training for the job is pronounced. A recent significant development is the incursion of the TTP in the Pakhtun areas as witnessed in the tragic July 6 attack on the Mangi Dam pumping station police post by the terrorist group, leading to the kidnapping and killing of 27 policemen. Our deliberations have led to identification of certain vulnerabilities and constraints that beset the police operating in the terror and insurgency-prone areas of KP and Balochistan where violence is driven by a combination of enhanced militant capability, difficult terrain, cross-border dynamics and institutional challenges. The following issues are pertinent. Intelligence coordination and information sharing: Coordination between police, intel agencies and other law-enforcement institutions is not always seamless; delays in sharing actionable intelligence reduce the ability to prevent attacks or intercept terrorists before they strike. Inadequate protection of police personnel and infrastructure: Police stations, check posts and patrols are often targeted because they have limited physical protection, surveillance or early-warning capabilities; some units in dangerous zones lack sufficient protective equipment, secure transport and modern communication systems, increasing their vulnerability. Limited capacity and community-based policing: In remote and conflict-affected areas, a trust deficit exists between communities and police. Without strong local engagement, authorities receive fewer timely reports about suspicious activities, allowing terrorist networks to operate with greater freedom. The merger of Fata into KP and the conversion of ‘B’ areas into ‘A’ areas in Balochistan was undertaken without adequate planning, capacity building or the provision of necessary financial and operational resources. The denial of these essential resources has exposed both police and the civil armed forces to avoidable risks, contributing to a significant increase in casualties among personnel. Expressions of support and appreciation for their sacrifices must therefore be matched by meaningful investment in manpower, training, equipment, intelligence, mobility and welfare to enable police to perform their duties effectively and safely. As former police chiefs we acknowledge that the challenges faced by current police commanders are far more daunting and require a strategic and operational rethink to restore order and promote peace in the restive borderlands in Pakistan’s north and south. Serving and retired police officers agree that the revised CT NAP must be implemented through professional tactics and strategic oversight. Here are a few recommendations at the operational level. Strengthen intelligence-led policing: Establish integrated intelligence coordination mechanisms that facilitate timely information-sharing among police, intelligence services and local administration; expand analytical capabilities and use technology to identify emerging threats, while ensuring operations remain consistent with the law and human rights standards. Modernise police protection and training: Upgrade security at vulnerable police facilities through better surveillance, convoy drills, ambush response, communications and sound infrastructure; provide regular training in CT tactics, drone threat response, incident command and officer safety, along with appropriate protective equipment. Expand community policing and public partnerships: Build stronger relationships with local communities, tribal elders, religious leaders and CSOs to improve trust and encourage lawful reporting of suspicious activities; develop accessible mechanisms for citizens to share information confidentially; promote public awareness programmes that strengthen resilience. The trend of rising terrorist attacks against, and thus higher casualties among, the police must be immediately stopped before it derails the entire CT effort in KP and Balochistan. This requires a balanced approach that combines effective policing, better intelligence coordination, professional training and meaningful community engagement. Strengthening these areas can enhance the safety of police personnel while also increasing public confidence and contributing to a more secure environment for local communities. Finally, for the policymakers and political leadership, our message is simple: invest in police and trust them to deliver. The writers are former inspectors-general of police. Published in Dawn, August 8th, 2026

items.title: La crisis de Ceuta cuestiona una frontera en la que Interior ha invertido más de 37 millones desde 2019
items.description: La crisis provocada el pasado 30 de julio por la entrada irregular de al menos 72.000 migrantes irregulares a nado en Ceuta ha puesto el foco en la supuesta vulnerabilidad de la frontera con Marruecos de esta ciudad autónoma. Un informe interno del Ministerio del Interior al que ha tenido acceso EL PAÍS detalla que desde 2019, tras la llegada de Pedro Sánchez al Palacio de La Moncloa, el Gobierno ha invertido 37,4 millones en la modernización y mejora del perímetro y los puestos fronterizos de esta localidad, y 42,7 millones en los de Melilla. En total, 80,1 millones de euros en proyectos ya ejecutados o en vía de ejecución, según el “balance financiero” incluido. El documento detalla que, antes de la tragedia que ha costado la vida a más de 80 personas en España , había previstas otras actuaciones por 99 millones en ambas localidades, la mayor parte para renovar viejas instalaciones de la Policía Nacional y de la Guardia Civil. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Los migrantes registrados por entidades sociales y organismos públicos en Ceuta superan con creces las cifras de Interior
items.description: “Ya está, no quedan más. Otra vez”, certifica una trabajadora de Cruz Roja en la playa del Trampolín de Ceuta. Entrega la última bolsa de plástico blanco con comida y agua, y agita los brazos en dirección al resto de migrantes que se apelotonaban en una cola caótica para recibir su ración y que hoy no comerán. “Lo siento, no hay más”, se excusa, alzando los brazos en señal de ausencia. Este jueves, la organización ha entregado más de 2.500 raciones, 500 más que los días anteriores, y siguen sin ser suficientes. En este trozo de costa, tanto la Policía que la custodia como los trabajadores humanitarios afirman que hay más de 2.000 personas, la mayoría subsaharianos. Una cifra que discute las dadas por el Ministerio del Interior, que el pasado martes aseguró que de las 72.000 personas que entraron en Ceuta, ya habían vuelto 70.000 a Marruecos, por lo que quedarían unas 2.000 en la ciudad. Una cifra que fuentes de Interior confirman que mantienen, porque no disponen de otros “datos fiables” que les permitan cambiarla, aunque subrayan su carácter estimativo. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Un barrido de las redes sociales marroquíes advierte de que la recluta de migrantes se ha vuelto menos visible pero sigue activa
items.description: La actividad de los grupos que reclutan migrantes para Ceuta y Melilla a través de las redes sociales en Marruecos se ha vuelto menos visible, pero sigue operativa. “La red [de reclutamiento] ha sido desplazada, pero no desmantelada. La actuación policial ha degradado la observabilidad [de los grupos que fomentan la migración ilegal] más rápido de lo que ha degradado su capacidad”, concluye el informe elaborado por la empresa Golden Owl, una startup vinculada al Parque Científico de la Universidad de Alicante. Seguir leyendo

items.title: El giro de Colombia
items.description: Colombia se suma al giro a la derecha que está cambiando gobiernos uno detrás de otro en el continente americano. Abelardo de la Espriella, un abogado sin trayectoria política previa, es desde este viernes el nuevo presidente. Sucede en el cargo a Gustavo Petro, que ha sido el primer presidente de izquierdas de la democracia colombiana. El cambio decidido por los colombianos en las urnas es grande: durante los próximos cuatro años, el país tendrá un Gobierno que promete políticas de libre mercado, mano dura contra la delincuencia y una visión conservadora en cuestiones sociales. La falta de antecedentes políticos de De la Espriella le ayudaron en su elección, al poder presentarse como ajeno a las estructuras del poder. Pero esa misma falta de credenciales arroja una sombra de incertidumbre sobre cómo administrará en la práctica un país de 50 millones de habitantes, una economía con crecimiento mediocre, hondos problemas de violencia y desigualdad y grandes expectativas de cambio. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Vivir el eclipse en una ‘star-party’ en Guadalajara con un astrónomo local: “Alguno incluso estallará en llanto”
items.description: La camiseta de Jaime Zamorano enumera los eclipses de sol que ha visto como si de una gira de conciertos se tratara: Venezuela, Francia, Libia, Australia, Isla de Pascua, China. “El espectáculo de un eclipse total no se puede comparar con nada”, dice el catedrático de astrofísica de la Complutense. “Estar a la sombra de la luna es una carambola cósmica que produce una sensación indescriptible”. Desde que se retiró de la docencia, disfruta de la vida rural en Villaverde del Ducado, pedanía de Alcolea del Pinar (Guadalajara), donde ahora tiene unas gallinas a las que grabará para ver la reacción que provoca en ellas el repentino anochecer. Seguir leyendo ¿Y tú, cómo vivirás el eclipse? En EL PAÍS, queremos saber cómo se preparan ustedes, nuestros lectores, para el fenómeno astronómico del 12 de agosto. Envíanos a participacion@elpais.es tu testimonio de cómo te preparas o cómo recibirá tu pueblo o ciudad el eclipse. Puedes incluir fotos si quieres. El próximo lunes, 10 de agosto, publicaremos algunas de las historias del eclipse de nuestros lectores.

items.title: Turismo con un exnarco: Laureano Oubiña vende un tour por donde colaba tabaco y hachís que la Xunta ve ilegal
items.description: A Laureano Oubiña no le importa que lo llamen rey del hachís , pero mira con lupa lo que los periodistas dicen de él, por si alguno se olvida de poner el “ex” antes que narco , aunque los jueces han tumbado todas sus demandas. “Tengo un jurado popular en Instagram con 85.000 seguidores y lo someto todo a su escrutinio para que opinen sobre lo que dicen de mí”, proclama Oubiña. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Mourinho y Guardiola, tan cerca y tan lejos
items.description: No hay constancia de que Pep Guardiola y José Mourinho hayan salido para comer juntos alguna vez, ni siquiera en Manchester, cuando eran vecinos, siempre separados por los dos clubes antagónicos de la ciudad a los que entrenaban: el City y el United. Igual que cuando el catalán dirigía al Barcelona y el portugués al Madrid y la distancia que mantenían era la misma que hay del Camp Nou al Bernabéu. La rivalidad llegó a ser tan enconada que partió el fútbol en dos bandos irreconciliables sin que los protagonistas hayan compartido nada más desde entonces que las condolencias por la muerte de uno de sus progenitores: Félix Mourinho y Dolors Sala. Nadie diría que mantuvieron una buena convivencia durante cuatro años en el Barça (1996-2000). Seguir leyendo

items.title: Playas de interior: ríos, pozas, embalses y otros lugares de baño que casi nunca aparecen en las guías
items.description: Vivo en Madrid, lejos de cualquier costa. Como tantos habitantes del interior, crecí sabiendo que el mar era un destino, algo que exigía planificación y kilómetros. Pero el deseo de agua no entiende de distancias y en verano ese deseo se resuelve de otra manera: en ríos, pozas, embalses y lagos, esos lugares de baño que casi nunca aparecen en las guías. Empecé creyendo que era un fenómeno de pueblos remotos, condenados por la geografía a inventarse su propio mar. Me equivocaba. Muchas veces la playa no está tan lejos y, aun así, la gente prefiere quedarse. Elige la poza de siempre, el recodo del río donde se bañaban sus padres, la orilla del embalse donde se reúnen los vecinos. Son lugares más cercanos, pero no en el sentido geográfico: más cercanos emocionalmente, más íntimos. Bañarse allí es una forma de estar en casa. Seguir leyendo

items.title: La misma crisis en Ceuta en un mundo diferente
items.description: Decía el gran sabio hispanoárabe Averroes que “la verdadera amistad no se mide por intereses temporales, sino que se bebe por amor gratuito”. Para el filósofo andalusí, los vecinos deben unirse, no por mera conveniencia económica sino por una autentica voluntad de procurar el bien común. Quizás esa sea la ausencia más elocuente en las relaciones entre España y Marruecos, y por extensión entre Europa y su frontera sur. La última crisis en Ceuta lo demuestra con una crudeza insoportable: más de 80 jóvenes muertos, muchos aún sin identificar; familias que siguen buscando desesperadamente a los suyos; miles de menores abandonados a su suerte. Este es el vergonzoso balance de esta tragedia. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Quién se emociona con un eclipse
items.description: Me pregunto desde dónde verá el eclipse total Andreas Karaolis, un fotógrafo que se pasa la vida viajando a lugares del mundo donde la noche es tan negra como la zona hadal, residencia habitual del pez diablo. Su especialidad es retratar cuerpos celestes. Gracias a su loable actividad en redes, he sabido que hay cámaras comerciales con las que cualquier ciudadano con pericia y presupuesto para plantarse en ubicaciones sin contaminación lumínica puede captar el esplendor multicapa y exuberante de la Vía Láctea. Seguir leyendo

items.title: ‘Adults Only’
items.description: La semana pasada, debatí con el dueño de una cadena de hoteles adults only , que es el eufemismo anglo que usan para no llamarlos hoteles que prohíben la entrada a los niños. Sus establecimientos alojan a perros y gatos, para los cuales hay un servicio de guardería, pero no a menores de 16 años. Lo hacen porque se les permite discriminar a un grupo social por motivos de edad y porque hay quien demanda espacios en los que se produzca esa discriminación. Es el mercado, amigo. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Si quiere ser feliz, no haga ‘mindfulness’
items.description: ¿Está usted sufriendo cierta depresión? ¿Padece tal vez de malas digestiones? ¿Le exaspera ir en metro? No se preocupe; todo lo que le molesta dejará de hacerlo si lo realiza conscientemente. El mindfulness le cambiará la vida, será un antes y un después. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Ayuso trata de borrar las huellas del ático con una venta precipitada y una obra inesperada
items.description: La compra de un ático de lujo por parte de la Comunidad de Madrid continúa envuelta en la bruma. Planifica Madrid, una empresa pública, lo adquirió por 6,3 millones en abril de manera opaca y sin dejar ningún rastro. Su existencia no se conocería si no la hubiera revelado EL PAÍS. El día que se supo, hace nueve días, la presidenta aseguró que iba a instalar en esa vivienda su despacho mientras durasen unas obras en la sede del Gobierno. Hasta ese momento nadie había oído hablar nunca de una supuesta remodelación en la Casa de Correos. Seguir leyendo

items.title: La escasez de munición del ejército estadounidense desata la ira de Trump
items.description: El presidente de Estados Unidos, Donald Trump , está furioso por el rápido descenso de las reservas de misiles de largo alcance en manos del ejército estadounidense y las consecuencias que eso puede tener para el desarrollo de la guerra en Irán, según varios medios estadounidenses. El republicano ha expresado su descontento por esta situación sobre la que ya fue alertado cuando comenzaron los primeros bombardeos sobre Teherán , hace casi seis meses. Seguir leyendo

items.title: El este de Alemania se rebela contra la reforma de las pensiones de Merz
items.description: Hay una tradición política en Alemania que se remonta al siglo XIX: los debates sin fin sobre las pensiones. El canciller Otto von Bismarck ya necesitó años de preparativos para tirar adelante en 1889 con el primer sistema público de jubilaciones del mundo. Es una cuestión recurrente que alimenta eternas discusiones parlamentarias, mediáticas y electorales. Era así hace siglo y medio y lo sigue siendo en 2026. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Pekín respalda la fuerza nuclear de Kim Jong-un
items.description: China ha dado un giro copernicano a la relación con su díscolo vecino norcoreano al respaldar su arsenal nuclear en lugar de empeñarse en la desnuclearización de la península coreana. En medio de una rivalidad global cada vez más feroz , Pekín ha tomado la capacidad nuclear de Pyongyang como un activo geopolítico que dificulta la posición de Estados Unidos en el noreste de Asia. Seguir leyendo

items.title: La sinrazón de seguir retrasando la aplicación de la ley de amnistía
items.description: La publicación de la sentencia del Tribunal de Justicia de la Unión Europea (TJUE) sobre la ley de amnistía ha reabierto debates que ya deberían estar superados y ha provocado en los tribunales actuaciones aparentemente contradictorias. Carece de sentido seguir demorando decisiones sobre el ámbito de aplicación de dicha ley, cuando el Tribunal Constitucional ha rechazado todos los recursos que se presentaron contra esta norma y una vez que la justicia europea no ha puesto objeciones, sino que ha apoyado su aplicación al resolver las dudas que le habían expuesto el Tribunal de Cuentas y la Audiencia Nacional . Seguir alargando los procedimientos abiertos en su día no favorece el pase de página y los propósitos de “reconciliación” que el propio tribunal de la UE ha atribuido al perdón a los líderes que en 2017 encabezaron el proyecto de ruptura de Cataluña con el resto de España. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Una boya de Mallorca bate el récord de calor en mar abierto del Mediterráneo con 33 grados
items.description: El Mediterráneo arde . El pasado miércoles se produjo un nuevo récord absoluto de temperatura de la superficie marina, en concreto en aguas españolas, en la boya de Sa Dragonera, al oeste de Mallorca, donde se llegó a las cuatro de la tarde a 33,2°, según las mediciones realizadas por Puertos del Estado y difundidas por la delegación territorial de la Agencia Estatal de Meteorología (Aemet) en Baleares a falta de confirmación oficial. Este dato es “una auténtica brutalidad”, en palabras del climatólogo, meteorólogo e investigador Samuel Biener a quien, como a todos los expertos, se le van agotando los adjetivos al hablar de calor. Seguir leyendo

items.title: El comité de empresa de Telemadrid denuncia la contratación “irregular” del chófer del director general
items.description: El conductor del director general de Telemadrid dejó de ser empleado de una empresa privada para convertirse, de un día para otro, en trabajador de la televisión pública madrileña . El cambio se produjo el pasado 15 de julio, cuando Radio Televisión Madrid (RTVM) lo incorporó a su plantilla pese a que el servicio de alquiler de vehículos con conductor seguía prestándose a través de un contrato público adjudicado a la empresa Auto Lavapiés. La contratación ha sido denunciada ante la Inspección de Trabajo por la sección sindical de CC OO (la mayoritaria) en representación del comité de empresa, que cuestiona tanto el procedimiento que se ha seguido para incorporar al trabajador como su exclusión del convenio colectivo de la corporación. Seguir leyendo

items.title: La última denuncia de Laura Cruz: “Tengo tanto miedo a Dámaso porque no le importa a quién llevarse por medio”
items.description: “Debo aclarar por qué tengo tanto miedo a Dámaso, no le importa a quién llevarse por medio, hasta prefiere perjudicarse él con tal de hacerme mal, de joderme la vida, como dijo literalmente en su momento y quedó probado en juicios anteriores”. Esta es parte de la declaración de Laura Cruz en la última denuncia que interpuso contra Dámaso Fernández , aunque le aterraba: “Denunciar estos hechos me causa pánico, no pudiendo descansar, quitándome las ganas de salir de casa, de no levantarme de la cama, llorando constantemente porque realmente no sé qué es mejor para mis hijos y para mí, aceptar su control y presión para que no nos haga nada o denunciar. Sé que esta denuncia le enfadará sin poder tener claras las consecuencias, pero no encuentro otra forma legal de defenderme frente al daño psicológico que ejerce sobre mí por todos los medios, ahora mediante el control patrimonial y económico, dañándome a mí y de nuevo a mis hijos”. Seguir leyendo

items.title: ¿Cómo hay que usar las gafas especiales durante el eclipse solar total del 12 de agosto?
Doce libros con mucha comida para leer en vacaciones: de Bourdain a Nora Ephron
items.description: Nos quedan unas semanas de verano por delante y con ello varias jornadas de descanso en posición horizontal en la playa, la piscina o el sofá. Sabemos que eres un apasionado de la gastronomía y que ni en vacaciones puedes dejar de pensar en ella, así que hemos vuelto a recopilar – también lo hicimos el año pasado – los libros que más nos han gustado al equipo Comidista recientemente que relatan, desde un ángulo o de otro, la comida. Entre ellos hay novelas, ensayos, memorias… eso sí, ningún recetario. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Leanne ten Brinke, psicóloga: “Hay tres veces más personalidades cercanas a la psicopatía en los altos cargos que en la población general”
items.description: Cuando escuchamos el concepto “ psicópata ”, lo primero que nos viene a la mente es la imagen de un asesino o un violador en serie, generalmente pasado por el filtro de las películas de Hollywood. Hannibal Lecter , el Javier Bardem de No es país para viejos, el Kevin Spacey de Seven… Sin embargo, sostiene la psicóloga social y de la personalidad Leanne ten Brinke (Antigonish, Nueva Escocia, Canadá, 40 años), vivimos rodeados de otras muchas personas que, sin alcanzar ni de lejos estas cotas de violencia extrema, sí que comparten con esos psicópatas que reinan en nuestro imaginario colectivo muchos rasgos de personalidad. Y esas personas pueden ser nuestro padre, nuestra pareja, nuestro amigo , nuestro jefe o quien dirige los designios de nuestro país. “Cada vez más, los psicólogos entienden la psicopatía y otros trastornos de la personalidad no como estados raros que no tienen nada que ver con una personalidad normal, sino como condiciones que revelan niveles extremos de rasgos de personalidad que, por lo demás, son normales”, explica a EL PAÍS por videollamada. Seguir leyendo

items.title: ¿Cómo consiguió Olivia Rodrigo caer bien a todo el mundo?
items.description: Hacía tiempo que en el universo de las grandes artistas del pop no brillaban tantas estrellas. De Taylor Swift a Madonna, pasando por Sabrina Carpenter o Charli xsx, estas divas llenan estadios y se hacen con el título de cabeza de cartel de festivales en los que hace años era impensable la música mainstream . Pese a la fuerza innegable del resto de compañeras, Olivia Rodrigo ha conseguido destacar gracias a su talento musical, su discurso y su personalidad. La californiana tiene una capacidad envidiable para caer bien incluso a aquellos que por edad o gustos no formarían parte de su público potencial. Con su último disco You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love ha despejado cualquier duda acerca de sus facultades y su poder de atracción. Seguir leyendo

items.description: Osun State Governor, Ademola Adeleke, charges residents to vote and defend their votes in the upcoming election, ensuring democratic rights are protected. Read More: https://punchng.com/defend-your-votes-adeleke-urges-osun-residents/

items.description: Lieutenant General Charles Costanza, commander of the US Army's V Corps, has been relieved of his command just two months before his scheduled departure, ABC News reports.

items.title: Danger ahead
items.description: PAKISTAN has already paid a heavy human price this monsoon, even as another dangerous spell approaches. NDMA figures covering June 26 to Aug 7 record 151 deaths — 73 of them children — and 448 injuries, besides damage to more than 1,200 houses and dozens of bridges and kilometres of roads. Chitral shows how quickly such destruction multiplies into other emergencies. Glofs, cloudbursts and flash floods have washed away bridges and severed roads, leaving communities unable to reach healthcare. Attendance at Lower Chitral’s district headquarters hospital has fallen by around 55pc, while patients from some isolated villages have stopped arriving altogether. Doctors are already reporting gastroenteritis and dysentery and fear outbreaks of typhoid and malaria. Pregnant women unable to reach hospitals face particular danger, while post-traumatic stress is emerging among disaster-hit communities. The situation shows us how extreme weather kills not only through torrents and collapsing homes, but also by cutting people off from medicines, clean water and timely treatment. NDMA, Rescue 1122, district administrations and the National Highway Authority have been involved in evacuations, relief distribution and restoration work. But each disaster exposes the distance between issuing warnings and protecting people. Chitral residents have complained of slow road clearance, delaying access to villages where medical needs are mounting. Warning equipment in parts of KP has previously been damaged or stolen, pointing to weaknesses in maintenance and local ownership. District authorities must know which settlements require evacuation, where residents will be taken, how alerts will get to people without mobile connectivity and how food, medicines and medical teams will reach communities. Such plans must be prepared before an emergency, not improvised after valleys are cut off. Medical camps, safe-water points and emergency stocks should be positioned in vulnerable valleys. There is particular urgency now. PMD’s Aug 7 outlook warns of moderate to heavy rainfall over the upper catchments of all major rivers from Aug 10 to 13, including KP, GB, Azad Kashmir, Islamabad and upper Punjab, with river and tributary flows expected to rise. Authorities should use this window to pre-position heavy machinery, boats, temporary bridges, fuel, food, drinking water, medicines and mobile clinics. Pregnant women, elderly people and patients requiring regular treatment should be identified for early evacuation, while alternative communication systems must be ready where conventional networks may fail. Shelters should be accessible and evacuation routes communicated before conditions deteriorate. Pakistan cannot control the monsoon or the instability of its glaciers. But it can control how seriously it acts on warnings. With the warning already given, the task now is to ensure that the next spell does not deepen an already heavy human toll. Published in Dawn, August 8th, 2026

items.title: ¿Es legal que los restaurantes prohíban la entrada a los ‘influencers’?
items.description: Los influencers gastronómicos son prescriptores digitales que convierten muchas veces la experiencia culinaria en un espectáculo para las redes. Sobre la mesa despliegan focos, luces y varios teléfonos sujetos a atriles; narran a viva voz, con micrófono en mano (la ultima moda), cada plato que llega y mastican frente a la cámara mientras explican sensaciones y sabores a sus seguidores. Lo que para algunos es una eficaz herramienta de promoción y publicidad, para otros supone una alteración del ambiente y una transformación de la gastronomía en mero contenido audiovisual. Son figuras que han ganado un gran protagonismo en la última década, debido a la ingente comunidad de seguidores que han conseguido crear en redes como Instagram, TikTok, YouTube o Facebook, capaz de convertir un restaurante desconocido en un fenómeno viral de la noche a la mañana, sin reparar en su carácter efímero. Seguir leyendo

items.title: El interés compuesto también ayuda a comprar una casa: cómo invertir para ahorrar el dinero de la entrada
items.description: Comprar una vivienda en España se ha convertido en una misión cada vez más complicada para muchas familias. La escasez de oferta, unida a la subida de los precios, impide a muchas personas, y especialmente a los más jóvenes, ahorrar el dinero necesario para la entrada a una casa. La mayoría de los bancos piden contar con al menos un 20% del precio del inmueble para conceder una hipoteca, al que hay que sumar impuestos y otros gastos. Para una vivienda de 300.000 euros, eso supone contar de antemano con 90.000, una cifra inalcanzable para la mayoría . Entre las opciones para reunir ese dinero, invertir puede ayudar a acelerar el proceso. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Govt restores original medical board for exhumation of Mir Raza’s body
items.description: • Corpse of IBA graduate to be dug up for fresh autopsy today • Exhumation planned for Friday postponed after family objected to abrupt reconstitution of board KARACHI: After a day of uncertainty over the exhumation of the body of IBA graduate and businessman Mir Raza Ali, the Sindh government on Friday evening restored the original medical board, which is set to exhume the body on Saturday (today). The exhumation, which was scheduled for Friday morning, was postponed after Raza’s family objected to the abrupt reconstitution of a medical board and inclusion of members from outside Karachi division. Raza’s body was found in bushes in Gulistan-i-Jauhar last month, a day after he went missing on July 28. On Thursday, a judicial magistrate had allowed the exhumation of the body on an application filed by Raza’s father, Mir Hussain Ali, directing the police surgeon and the Sindh health secretary to constitute a medical board for the exhumation. The Sindh health department then constituted an eight-member board, with Police Surgeon Dr Summaiya Syed as the convener. Prof Dr Naseem Ahmed of Dow University of Health Sciences, Dr Farah Waseem of Jinnah Sindh Medical University, Amir Hassan Khan of Citizens Police Liaison Committee, Additional Police Surgeon Dr Sirichand, Dr Kamran Khan and Dr Daniyal Mirza of Jinnah Postgraduate Medical Centre and Dr Mohammed Yaseen, the admin in-charge of the police surgeon office, were the other members of the board. However, in the small hours of Friday morning, the board was reconstituted through an order issued by the director general of the Sindh health department. While Dr Syed remained the convener of the new five-member board, its members were changed to Prof Dr Zakiuddin from DUHS, Prof Dr Kazi Akbar and Prof Dr Abid Hussain Chang from Liaquat University of Medical and Health Sciences and Hyderabad Police Surgeon Dr Waseem Khan. On Friday morning, Raza’s family was present at the Tariq Road graveyard for the exhumation. But, the exhumation was deferred, with the counsel for Raza’s family, Jibran Nasir, telling the media that they had informed the investigating officer that the family had rejected the reconstituted board and would not accept an exhumation by it “under any circumstances”. Standing alongside Raza’s father, Advocate Nasir accused the authorities of trying to bury the facts and held the police, health department and the Sindh government responsible for the delay. The family could not allow the exhumation to be performed by members whose “qualifications and intentions were under question”, he added. He recalled that the previous night, DG-health dismissed the original board and reconstituted it, adding four names from Hyderabad. He claimed that following outcry over the reconstituted board, the DG-health then issued a “backdated notification at around 10am on Friday, stating that more members may be added, but the four chosen by him should also remain a part of it”. He added that they still had not been informed why the original board was reconstituted. The lawyer said they would not be making any demands to the police. Raza’s father was now directly raising questions to Sindh Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah and PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari, he said. He asserted that they only trusted the original eight-member board, adding, “Sindh government, they were hired by you. And if they are not competent enough, then how were they appointed in the first place?” Advocate Nasir also submitted a letter to the police surgeon on Friday, wherein he formally informed her of the family’s non-consent and stated that the reconstituted board was in “complete violation and negation” of the court’s order and had no legal basis. He held that it carried no binding value and was nothing “but a malicious attempt to interfere with judicial proceedings initiated by the court” and any directive in support of the board shall be viewed as a “further malicious attempt to provide cover to an illegal act and sabotage fair and transparent investigation”. He said the family had not consented to the exhumation by the reconstituted board and warned that any attempt to proceed with the exhumation under the reconstituted medical board will be a violation of the dignity of the deceased, will put evidence at risk and will be a “blatant” contempt of court. Late in the evening, the Sindh health secretary issued a notification, restoring the original eight-member medical board. Following the notification, the police surgeon sent a letter to the magistrate concerned and other members of the board, informing them that the exhumation is risk and will be a “blatant” contempt of court. Late in the evening, the Sindh health secretary issued a notification, restoring the original eight-member medical board. Following the notification, the police surgeon sent a letter to the magistrate concerned and other members of the board, informing them that the exhumation is scheduled to be conducted at the graveyard adjacent to Rehmania Masjid at 11am on Saturday (today). Prior to the restoration of the original medical board, the police surgeon expressed her frustration over “impediments” in a post on X. The post was deleted after the government restored the eight-member board. It may be noted that the case took a new turn when the police surgeon told a private news channel on Tuesday that the post-mortem findings had raised several questions, as some observations in the report did not appear to match the available photographs. Her interview prompted the police authorities to issue a statement, terming such observations as having the potential to adversely affect the ongoing investigation. items.title: Hunter Biden says his pardon was ‘not good’ for America or his father’s legacy
items.description: Hunter Biden has told the BBC he is “the most privileged person there is” after receiving a presidential pardon from his father, former US President Joe Biden, acknowledging it was not a good choice for America or his father’s legacy. In a wide-ranging interview with the BBC’s Newsnight, Hunter Biden defended the controversial pardon, reflected on his father’s declining health, ruled out seeking elected office and spoke about helping others recover from addiction. Asked about the 2024 pardon, he said he understood the criticism but noted: “What would you have thought of my dad if he did not do that for me.” “It’s something that is easily criticised and for good reason,” he added. “It’s not fair… All I know is that I’m grateful that he did it for me,” he said, acknowledging the pardon was “not good” for the American people, the Constitution – or his father’s legacy. He argued to the BBC that his father ultimately acted out of concern that he would become a target under Donald Trump’s incoming administration. “I was the only one in the world that could have gotten what I got from the only person in the world who could give it, my father.” Hunter Biden also insisted he and his father had never discussed the possibility of a pardon before it was granted. “There is no way that you can have those kinds of discussions that would not become public,” he said. President Biden granted his son a full and unconditional pardon in December 2024, despite repeatedly saying beforehand that he would not use the powers of the presidency to intervene in his son’s legal cases. In announcing the decision, the former president said his son had been “selectively and unfairly prosecuted”. The pardon covered his son’s federal gun conviction, a tax case he’d pled guilty to and any federal offences committed between 2014 and 2024. Hunter Biden got emotional at times in the interview, notably when discussing his father’s health. Cancer is really hard,” he said, stopping to clear his throat. “It’s really sad to watch.” “My dad is, to this day, the centre of our family,” he said. “He’s the best father, the best husband, the best grandfather.” He said Joe Biden’s cancer had spread, describing it as “very painful” and “very debilitating”. “The only thing that I say about my dad, about his health right now, is I wish he would complain more.” Hunter Biden also reflected on the presidential debate in June 2024 that ultimately ended his father’s re-election campaign. He said he had watched it from his home in California and immediately sensed something was wrong. “I was shocked,” he said. “I knew something was wrong.” Hunter Biden has previously argued that his father’s poor debate performance reflected physical exhaustion after extensive travel. Following Joe Biden’s cancer diagnosis, he has also questioned whether the illness may already have been affecting his father. He said his father remains politically engaged and determined to continue speaking publicly. When asked about rumours that he might enter politics – or even make a run for the presidency – Biden said he himself had “no interest in elected politics” and dismissed any suggestion that he would one day seek office. Instead, Biden said he wanted to devote his time to speaking about addiction and recovery, which he described as a cause capable of bridging America’s political divides. “I believe that addiction and the hope of recovery are something that connect us all,” he said. Asked what made him proudest of his father, Hunter Biden pointed not to his years in public office but to his resilience. “I’m most proud of his resilience,” he said. “He’s proven time and time again that when you get knocked down, you can get up. “He’s the toughest man I know.”

items.title: Espagne: Luca Zidane quitte Grenade et rejoint Leganes en D2
items.description: Le gardien international algérien, Luca Zidane, fils du nouveau sélectionneur des Bleus, Zinedine Zidane, a rejoint Leganes en provenance de Grenade, ont annoncé les deux clubs de D2 espagnole. Le portier de 28 ans s'est engagé pour une saison avec le club basé dans la communauté de Madrid, assortie d'une saison supplémentaire en option. Grenade a de son côté expliqué avoir « conclu un accord (avec le joueur) pour mettre fin à la relation contractuelle qui les unissait » après 45 apparitions de Zidane en deux saisons. Le Franco-Algérien poursuit ainsi sa carrière en deuxième division espagnole, lui qui a également évolué au Racing Santander (2019), au Rayo Vallecano (2020-22, participant à sa montée en Liga) et à Eibar (2022-24). Formé au centre de formation du Real, qu'il a rejoint en 2004 à l'âge de six ans, Luca Zidane a auparavant porté les couleurs du Real Madrid avec l'équipe réserve avant de faire ses débuts avec l'équipe première lors de la dernière journée de Liga de la saison 2017-18, sous les ordres de son père, alors sur le banc. Après avoir représenté la France dans les catégories jeunes, Luca Zidane est devenu international algérien l'année dernière et a participé en tant que titulaire à la Coupe du monde 2026 avec les Fennecs, dont le parcours s'est achevé en 16e de finale face à la Suisse (2-0). items.title: Can Tinubu dvice Governors On What He Controls? By Emmanuel Aziken
items.description: President Bola Tinubu’s extraordinary intervention in the freezing of an Osun State Government account by the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission has brought into sharp relief a question that has increasingly shadowed his presidency: who exactly acts in the President’s name, and how much of what is done around him carries his prior knowledge and approval? The EFCC had secured a court order restricting withdrawals from an Osun State statutory allocation account as part of an investigation into the alleged fraudulent handling of about N11 billion in Ecology Funds, Intervention Funds and FAAC allocations. Coming barely days before the August 15 governorship election, however, the action inevitably acquired a political colour. Tinubu apparently recognised the danger. In a personally signed statement, he directed the EFCC to return to court immediately to vacate the order. He said he was “deeply embarrassed”, not by the commission performing its statutory duty, but by the timing of the action, and stressed that no federal institution should create the impression that Abuja was trying to influence the Osun election. That distinction is important. The President did not absolve Governor Ademola Adeleke’s administration of any allegation under investigation. Neither did he order the EFCC to abandon its statutory responsibilities. What he did was insist that law enforcement must not become indistinguishable from partisan warfare. In the circumstances, it was the correct intervention. Osun is particularly sensitive terrain for Tinubu. The state is one where his APC has suffered two politically significant defeats in recent years. Adeleke defeated incumbent APC Governor Gboyega Oyetola in 2022, polling 403,371 votes against Oyetola’s 375,027. Months later, in the 2023 presidential election, Tinubu lost Osun to the PDP’s Atiku Abubakar, who polled 354,366 votes against Tinubu’s 343,945. The political confrontation therefore has history behind it. It became even more complicated by the crisis within the PDP and Adeleke’s flirtation with the APC. Adeleke’s camp has publicly maintained that he did not reject an invitation to join the APC but that his movement was resisted by Oyetola and the Osun APC establishment. Adeleke eventually moved to Accord, on whose platform he is seeking re-election. For some within the APC, the calculation may have appeared straightforward: with the PDP weakened and federal power behind the ruling party, Adeleke could be politically overwhelmed. That calculation underestimates the governor. Whatever assessment anyone makes of Adeleke’s record in office, he belongs to one of Nigeria’s most enduring political families. His father, Senator Raji Ayoola Adeleke, an ally of Chief Obafemi Awolowo, was elected to the Senate on the Unity Party of Nigeria platform during the Second Republic. His elder brother, Isiaka Adeleke, became Osun’s first civilian governor in 1992 and subsequently served twice in the Senate. Ademola himself represented Osun West in the Senate before becoming governor. That is political infrastructure accumulated across generations. Then there is the Adeleke family’s extraordinary cultural reach. Governor Adeleke’s nephew, Davido, is one of Africa’s most recognisable music stars and gives the family access to a youthful constituency that conventional politicians would pay heavily to cultivate. Celebrity cannot substitute for organisation or performance, but in a close election its mobilisation value should not be dismissed. Tinubu’s intervention consequently does more than rescue Osun from a potentially destabilising confrontation days before an election. It also protects the President himself. The more troubling question is how such a politically explosive action came to be taken at such a politically explosive moment before presidential intervention became necessary. The EFCC is an institution with statutory responsibilities and had obtained a court order. Yet the President’s public embarrassment over the timing raises legitimate questions about political judgment and coordination within the federal establishment. It would be reckless to conclude, without evidence, that “rogue elements” deliberately engineered the affair in Tinubu’s name. But it is reasonable to ask whether officials around the presidency and federal institutions sufficiently appreciate that their actions can carry consequences for the President’s credibility. Tinubu therefore has a larger assignment than merely extinguishing the Osun fire. Where federal institutions repeatedly take controversial steps that force the President into public reversals or damage his political standing, he must establish who authorised what, on what information and with what appreciation of the consequences. Accountability cannot stop at correcting decisions after public outrage. There is a biblical injunction in Proverbs 25:5: “Remove the wicked from the king’s presence, and his throne will be established through righteousness.” The principle remains relevant to political leadership. A ruler is ultimately judged not only by his intentions but also by the conduct of those exercising authority around him. Tinubu has acted wisely in Osun by insisting that the August 15 election must not carry the stain of federal interference. The APC is entitled to campaign vigorously for Bola Oyebamiji. Adeleke is equally entitled to defend his mandate. The EFCC is entitled to investigate credible allegations. But the people of Osun alone must decide who governs them. If Tinubu wants this intervention to count towards his legacy, he must go beyond Osun. He should ensure that nobody, whether political ally, presidential aide or federal official, can weaponise the enormous authority of the Nigerian state for partisan purposes. The best “fix” for Osun is therefore not an APC victory or an Adeleke victory. It is a credible election whose outcome cannot reasonably be attributed to Abuja. That would be a victory for Tinubu too. The post Can Tinubu dvice Governors On What He Controls? By Emmanuel Aziken appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: NAB chief urges withdrawal of Rs500m graft probe limit
items.description: • Tells Senate panel bureau’s hands are tied under amended law to act against govt officials • Says private sector accounts for 45pc of corruption ISLAMABAD: The National Account­abi­lity Bureau (NAB) on Friday urged the government to withdraw a restriction that prevents it from taking action against government officials accused of corruption involving less than Rs500 million. “Untie our hands and withdraw the Rs500m restriction; otherwise, people [government officials] will become addicted to committing corruption,” NAB Chairman retired Lt Gen Nazir Ahmed said during a meeting of the Senate Standing Committee on Law and Justice. Under the amended NAB law, the anti-graft watchdog cannot take up cases involving amounts below Rs500m. As a result, a large number of cases it had been pursuing were transferred to other departments, such as the Federal Investigation Agency. Mr Ahmed said that because of the restriction, a station house officer (SHO) of the police enjoyed more powers than a NAB investigation officer. A NAB prosecutor general read out the amended law governing the anti-graft body, saying the bureau could not take action against members of the federal or provincial cabinets or their committees. At this, committee chairman Senator Farooq Naek said that although NAB could not act against cabinet decisions or those of its committees, it could proceed against individuals who violated those decisions or engaged in corrupt practices. He said NAB had been established to investigate mega corruption cases, such as the Rs1.20 trillion Neelum-Jhelum Hydropower Project, on which Rs513bn had been spent. It had now emerged, he said, that the design prepared by the National Engineering Services Pakistan (Nespak) was faulty. “It is a joke played on the people of Pakistan. We all know that corruption was committed during the construction of roads,” he added. JUI-F Senator Kamran Murtaza, also a member of the committee, said the Rs500m threshold should also be withdrawn in cases involving politicians. The NAB chairman said the media usually highlighted cases involving politicians more vigorously than other corruption cases. However, he said politicians accounted for six per cent of the country’s overall corruption, while government officials were responsible for 11pc. ‘Private sector’ “We are always asked to pursue cases against politicians. However, the private sector, including the sugar mafia, accounts for more than 45pc of the country’s total corruption,” he added. The committee chairman asked why NAB did not take action against officials of the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) and the police. Mr Ahmed replied that the FBR did not fall within NAB’s jurisdiction. Senator Abdul Qadir urged NAB to investigate the petroleum sector, where wells had been drilled for oil and gas exploration over the past 20 years without any production. “If NAB takes action on this, millions of people could benefit from cheaper oil and gas,” he added. The committee also received a detailed briefing from NAB, during which its chairman claimed the bureau had recovered assets worth $64bn, including state and private land. Published in Dawn, August 8th, 2026

items.title: Killer Cops: DCI reveals officer who pulled trigger in Dr Mutiso assassination
Making your roots proud of you, by Muyiwa Adetiba
items.description: All Igbobians – students of Igbobi College – must know about the big fruit tree between the Dining Hall and the Chapel. This tree has been there like forever serving as a rendezvous of sorts for many school events. I believe it is one of the fixtures that can tell the story of the school. Some forty-five years ago, a handful of Old Igbobians met there for an event. I remember it was early evening and visibility was low. We were asked to introduce ourselves by stating name, set, house and the sports we participated in while in school. It was not an uncommon ritual. I had just finished this chore when I heard a voice behind me say ‘so Muyiwa Adetiba came to Igbobi. No wonder.’ I looked back in surprise to identify the voice. It was from an older man, probably a senior who had left school before I entered. I met a warm smile as I nodded my head in acknowledgement and respect. Honestly, it was at the time, one of the best compliments I had received in years. All true Old Igbobians would know why. The moral and intellectual standards set by the school were high and this seemingly off-handed compliment, was for me, a tacit acknowledgement, that I had at least, met some of them. I was to be a proud recipient of a few ‘no wonder’ comments from Old Igbobians during my years as an interviewer. Some of them were probably in school about the time I was born. Quite a few willingly helped me to get difficult interviews by either using their connections or vouching for me. A good example was Chief Chris Ogunbanjo, an Old Igbobian, whose vouching for me overcame the understandable reluctance of Chief Justice Fatai Williams when I wanted to interview him immediately after the Supreme Court judgement on Chief Obafemi Awolowo’s presidential bid. Another notable ‘endorsement’ came about ten years ago after I had more or else rested my pen. Someone I have a great respect for, an Old Igbobian whom I never met in school, approached me to help a prominent Nigerian with his memoirs. I don’t just jump into working on anybody’s memoirs. For me, it is a labor of love that I have to be able to invest emotionally in. Fortunately, this prominent Nigerian was someone I had admired from afar so it wasn’t difficult to accept. Unknown to me, this great man was reluctant. His fear was that he had sensitive stories he wanted to be careful in divulging. When he was told that I was not only a fellow Old Igbobian, I was like him, the school’s Merit Award recipient, he said ‘oh, that is good enough for me”. Those seven words meant the world to me. People normally trust those they have had a good relationship with. In his own case, he was prepared to trust me with sensitive documents because we shared the same Alma Mater. I have issued a few ‘no wonder’ comments of my own as well when I hear or read about the accomplishments of some distinguished Nigerians and I go through their CV to discover that they passed through the portals of Igbobi College. Most of them were in academia and the professions; hardly in government. In fact, we used to lament that Igbobi College didn’t prepare us for the intrigues and duplicities in governance. A welcome departure was Babatunde Fashola, whom I had long admired for his elocution and intellect until I found he had a stint at Igbobi College and my ‘no wonder’ comment came out. Of course anybody would be proud to share school colors with Professor Yemi Osinbajo, a junior in whom I have always been well pleased. I have also found myself to be more relaxed and trusting of people just because we share the same Alma Mater. This sentiment is not peculiar to Old Igbobians alone. Many Old Boys of Kings College, St Gregory’s College and the Government Colleges all over the country, share this sentiment too. Underpinning the sentiment is the belief that if you were good enough to pass through the four walls of their school, you were good enough. Yoruba parents require of their children to ‘remember the child of whom they are’. if I have heard it once, I have heard it countless times. It is an admonition not to stain the family name or cast it into aspersion. It stems from the belief that a good name is better than wealth and a good pedigree is worth its weight in gold. To many, this administration is the face of Yoruba. But in reality, it is more personal as it is the fulfilment of someone’s ‘emilokan’. It is not surprising that many a true ‘Omoluabi’ will find it difficult to identify with or be proud of some of the goings on in this government. The question must be asked if this administration Is cleaning up the mess left by past administrations or adding a few of its own. Is it wiping the glass clean or smudging it? is it the best we can be? That is, if this administration is really the face of Yoruba as some people mischievously claim. I feel particularly pained about the PFIPC scam that would not go away because Femi Gbajabiamila, one of the men in the eye of the storm, is both Yoruba and an Old Igbobian. Although he didn’t meet me in school, I still share vicariously in his successes and his failures. He needs to clear his name. For his sake. For the sake of all of us who identify with his roots one way or another. He is presumed innocent until proven guilty and evidences adduced so far point more to systemic failures and systemic abuse than to him. He possesses the intellect, the elocution and the confidence of an Igbobian. Enough to say ‘no wonder’. But Igbobi College was never about intellect alone. Character has always been important, if not more important. In our time, Aggrey House, my House, made all Form One students to memorise the poem ‘IF’ by Rudyard Kipling. The poem is about what it takes to be a man of character. Igbobi College is about molding a boy into a man of nobility who will be a light unto the world. Which is why the most important line in the school song is ‘wherever there is an Igbobian, there also is a noble Nigerian’. Which is why we sometimes refer to ourselves as ‘the Noble One’. Finally, if those in the public space thought more about their names and their roots than money and instant gratification, there would be less of these scams and Nigeria would begin to turn around for good. The post Making your roots proud of you, by Muyiwa Adetiba appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Broad Peak search for bodies of 3 climbers paused
items.description: • Mission to resume once weather improves • Bodies of Nirmal Purja, four other foreign climbers flown to Islamabad for repatriation to their respective countries GILGIT: The search operation to recover the remains of Pakistani mountaineer Sohail Sakhi and two foreign climbers missing after the deadly Broad Peak avalanche has been suspended due to the continuing risk of fresh avalanches, rescue officials said on Friday. Search teams spent eight days trying to locate the rem­ains of Sohail Sakhi, American climber Sarah Mallory Geis, and Nepalese climber Nawang Thindu Sherpa before deteriorating conditions forced authorities to halt the mission. Ayaz Shigri, General Secre­t­a­­ry of the Alpine Club of Pakistan (ACP), said a leg believed to belong to Geis had earlier been recovered. He added that Nawang Thindu Sherpa’s body has been located but cannot be retrieved because it lies in a highly dangerous, avalanche-prone area. He said rescue efforts would resume once weather conditions improve and the area is safe. ACP President Major Gen-eral (retd) Irfan Arshad Khan also confirmed the suspension, saying rescue teams would return to Broad Peak when conditions permit. Meanwhile, the bodies of five foreign climbers killed in the Bro­ad Peak avalanche were flown from Skardu to Islamabad on a private airline flight on Fri­day for repatriation. They were received by Airport Mana­ger Aftab Ali Shah Gillani, ASF Chief Security Officer Mu­­ham­mad Rashid, and other officials before being transfer­red to the mortuary at the Pims, where they will remain until repatriation arrangements are completed. The bodies had been airlifted from Broad Peak Base Camp to Skardu and temporarily kept at the CMH, Skardu. Mr Khan said the deceased climbers were wrap­ped in their national flags bef­o­­re being handed over to airport au­­thorities by the Pakistan Army. The remiains of three climbers will be repatriated to Nepal, while Purja’s body will be sent to the UK. Meanwhile, Chinese climber Zhong’s family is expected in Islamabad to collect his body. With input from Mohammad Asghar Published in Dawn, August 8th, 2026

items.title: Watchdogs call for scrapping foreign press curbs
items.description: KARACHI: As concern grows over recent restrictions imposed on foreign media outlets operating in the country, global human rights watchdogs have termed the fresh guidelines issued by the government “an attack on press freedom”. Until the new government restrictions were first circulated widely over the weekend, only foreign citizens working as journalists were routinely subject to controls on movement outside Islamabad, Lahore and Karachi. Now, Pakistani journalists, fixers and others working for foreign media will need government permission to travel and report outside those three major cities and must register with the government – even for leisure travel. The controls mark “an alarming step” in Pakistan’s “narrowing space for press freedom,” said Patricia Gossman of Human Rights Watch, calling for them to be “immediately reversed”. Meanwhile, Amnesty International said on Friday that the restrictions on foreign news outlets, extending to local staff of these organisations, under the new Foreign Media Facilitation Guidelines, 2026 were “an attack on press freedom”. “Why is the government afraid of truth?,” the statement questioned. Earlier, the New York-based Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) had called on authorities to withdraw what it termed “draconian new guidelines”. “The Foreign Media Facilitation Guidelines open the door for Pakistani authorities to further restrict international media coverage, prevent journalists from reporting freely outside Pakistan’s three main cities, and risk exposing them to administrative retaliation,” CPJ Afghanistan and Pakistan Representative Waliullah Rahmani said in a statement. The Human Rights Commission of Pakistan, and the country’s main journalist union, the Pakistan Federal Union of Journalists, have already condemned the ‘Foreign Media Facilitation Guidelines 2026’. According to CPJ, the five-page guidelines were introduced days after the government criticised international reporting on elections and protests in Azad Kashmir and accused Al Jazeera of engaging in “yellow journalism,” a term for sensational reporting. Subsequently, foreign media representatives were ordered out of Azad Kashmir earlier this week. The Financial Times , one of several outlets operating in Pakistan, told Reuters it “supports the ability of journalists to report freely and independently.” A spokesperson for Reuters said, “Journalists should be free to report the news wherever they are.” In a statement, the BBC also said it was “extremely concerned” about the new guidelines, and called on Pakistani authorities to reverse the “unnecessary restrictions”. “Freedom of the press is increasingly under pressure around the world and this unwelcome change in approach is a step backwards for Pakistan’s media freedom,” a spokesperson for the broadcaster said in a statement. According to New York Times , Pakistan ranks 153rd out of 180 countries in the Repo­rters Without Borders’ Press Freedom Index. Published in Dawn, August 8th, 2026

items.title: Spain to impose border controls against Italy as row over Ceuta migrant influx intensifies
items.description: Spain will impose border controls on all air and sea travel from Italy as a row between the two EU countries intensifies. The measures – coming into force at midnight (22:00 GMT) and lasting for a month – come a week after Italy introduced similar restrictions following an influx of about 78,000 migrants from Morocco into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta. On Friday, Spain demanded Italy reverse its checks by Sunday. Rome said they would stay until at least 15 August – when, according to it, Spain “expects a new wave of migration” to hit Ceuta. The crisis has pitted Spain’s socialist leader Pedro Sanchez against Italy’s conservative leader Giorgia Meloni – who has long called for stricter EU migration rules. Italy does not share a land border with Spain. Its government said last week that decision to temporarily suspend the ​border-free Schengen arrangement was to prevent any of the migrants who had entered Ceuta from travelling on to Italy. Madrid dismissed this position, saying it was based on “spurious arguments” that lacked any basis in fact because the migrants who entered Ceuta had no way of entering the Schengen area. In its response to the Spanish threat earlier on Friday, Italy’s government said it would not accept “ultimatums”. It added that it did not intend “under any circumstances to reconsider the decision to suspend the application of the Schengen Agreement for third-country nationals arriving from Spain, at least until August 15th and in any case until security and terrorist risks for Italy have been completely eliminated”. Italian officials have said local authorities carrying out checks do “everything possible” to ensure maximum comfort for both Spanish and other European citizens arriving in Italy from Spain. Rome has also reiterated that Spanish citizens are exempt from additional checks when arriving in Italy, with these extra steps only for non-EU residents. However, El Pais reported that several airport terminals have seen long queues and waiting times in recent days, with passengers arriving from Spain directed to a specific line for checks. The counter-measures Madrid decided to impose on Friday would include passport, nationality and visa checks for Italian passengers and visitors from other countries arriving from Italy “amid the persistent irregular migratory pressure” the country was experiencing, a statement from Spain’s government said. Checks would stay in place until 7 September “unless a change in the circumstances that led to its adoption warrants modifying that period”. Temporary suspensions of the Schengen agreement are not unprecedented. Italy also maintains controls on its border with Slovenia. Italy’s decision to suspend Schengen for a month was backed by Finland and Denmark, while the Czech Republic called for Spain’s membership to be temporarily suspended. Most of the migrants who arrived in Ceuta last week were returned within days. Nearly 1,400 minors, some of them “very young boys and girls”, still remain there. Spain has not announced an anticipated second wave of crossings from Morocco. Reports have been fuelled by social media activity by Moroccan users planning another attempt, El Pais reports. The Spanish prime minister’s office told the newspaper they were monitoring the situation but did not expect a repeat of scenes from last week. It remains unclear exactly why tens of thousands of migrants attempted to cross into Ceuta, but the EU’s Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner has suggested criminal networks spreading disinformation were to blame – an assertion the Spanish government has agreed with. The crossings came after Spain’s Supreme Court ruled that migrants stopped at sea while trying to reach Ceuta or Melilla cannot be summarily returned to Morocco. Morocco, for its part, has laid blame for the crisis on the court, with an unnamed government source briefing local outlets that “the deterrent element of the system collapsed and the dam gave way, not under the weight of the criminals, but of a judge’s decision”. The number of people swimming to Ceuta at once has raised questions about why Morocco’s border guards did not attempt to stop them. The two exclaves have long been a bone of diplomatic contention between Spain and Morocco, which does not recognise Spanish sovereignty over them.
