items.title: Infrastructure vandalism: Scavengers threaten Lagos bridge, 27 arrested
items.description: By Olasunkanmi Akoni LAGOS — The Lagos State Government has uncovered alleged vandalism of critical infrastructure beneath the newly constructed bridge linking Festac Town with the Alakija area of Amuwo-Odofin Local Government Area of the state. The discovery was made during a special enforcement operation conducted by state government agencies in line with the directive of Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu to rid the Lagos-Badagry Transnational Highway of infractions, environmental pollution, illegal motor parks, roadside trading and unauthorised activities on highway setbacks and pedestrian walkways. The State Commissioner for the Environment and Water Resources, Tokunbo Wahab, disclosed the development on Friday through his official X handle. According to Wahab, preliminary investigations indicated that suspected vandals, including scavengers, had allegedly removed iron rods, steel reinforcements, cables and other materials from beneath the bridge. He said the alleged removal of the materials could compromise the structural integrity of the infrastructure and pose a safety concern to members of the public. “This criminal act poses a serious threat to public safety and undermines the government’s investment in critical infrastructure,” Wahab stated. Following the discovery, a joint midnight enforcement operation involving officers of the Rapid Response Squad (RRS) and the Kick Against Indiscipline (KAI) task force was launched at the location. The operation resulted in the arrest of 27 suspects, who Wahab said would be prosecuted in accordance with the extant laws of Lagos State. “The Lagos State Government remains committed to protecting public infrastructure and will continue to take decisive action against individuals or groups engaged in acts of vandalism, environmental infractions and other criminal activities that threaten the safety and wellbeing of residents,” he said. Residents condemn alleged vandalism Some residents who reacted to the development condemned the alleged vandalism and called for stricter enforcement and appropriate punishment for offenders. A resident identified as @Primax2U said government should also address some of the socio-economic factors that could encourage people to engage in scavenging and other activities to make a living. “As much as it’s bad destroying government property and risking lives, government needs to also assist in subsidising basic amenities or, better still, create job opportunities that would definitely remove more idle minds to more productive things than destruction to make a living,” the resident said. Another resident, identified as @tycityevents, expressed concern over the alleged removal of structural materials from beneath the bridge. “We have some terrible people in Lagos. How can anyone dig deep beneath a bridge just to remove the steel reinforcement rods? If urgent action isn’t taken, this bridge could be at serious risk,” the resident stated. Third Mainland Bridge The latest incident recalls similar cases of alleged vandalism reported on the Third Mainland Bridge, where suspects were arrested in connection with the removal of newly installed infrastructure. The Third Mainland Bridge has previously been targeted by vandals, with reports of the theft and destruction of safety installations, including solar-powered reflective road studs and bridge railings. Authorities subsequently intensified surveillance and patrols around the bridge, with CCTV systems also deployed to assist in identifying and tracking suspected offenders. The removal of road studs and reflective lighting installations can reduce visibility for motorists, particularly at night, potentially increasing road safety risks. The incidents have prompted condemnation from government officials and calls for stronger surveillance and protection of public infrastructure across Lagos. The post Infrastructure vandalism: Scavengers threaten Lagos bridge, 27 arrested appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Defence Minister-designate Adjei must prioritise GAF personnel welfare — KAIPTC lecturer
items.description: Security lecturer at the Kofi Annan International Peacekeeping Training Centre (KAIPTC), Dr Victor Doke, has urged Defence Minister-designate Kenneth Gilbert Adjei to make the welfare of personnel of the Ghana Armed Forces his foremost priority if approved by Parliament. Dr Doke made the remarks following President John Dramani Mahama’s decision to reassign Mr Adjei from the Ministry of Works, Housing and Water Resources to the Ministry of Defence. The appointment comes nearly a year after the death of Defence Minister Dr Edward Omane Boamah, who was among those killed in a military helicopter crash. President Mahama has submitted Mr Adjei’s nomination to Parliament through the Speaker for prior approval, in accordance with Article 78(1) of the 1992 Constitution. Speaking on the responsibilities awaiting the minister-designate, Dr Doke said addressing the welfare of military personnel should be at the centre of his agenda. READ ALSO: Mahama names Kenneth Gilbert Adjei as Defence Minister to replace late Omane Boamah “The welfare generally of the armed forces is a particular issue, is a top priority as at now, and housing, remuneration, promotions, the gender issues are top notch.” According to him, improving accommodation, remuneration, career progression and addressing gender-related concerns within the Armed Forces will be critical to strengthening morale and operational effectiveness. Dr Doke also said the minister-designate faces a significant task in succeeding his predecessor and will need to draw on the experience of both the military leadership and former officials to succeed. “It’s one of the issues which Honourable Gilbert would have to tackle as much as possible. He has a big, big, big position now, big shoes to fill. He needs to court all the cooperation and collaboration from the military hierarchy, past leaders of that specific agency and then get the ideas, the knowledge to be able to roll out the initiatives that he wants and then the objectives of the President for the Ghana Armed Forces.” He expressed confidence that the military’s leadership would support the incoming minister, regardless of who occupies the position, provided there is mutual respect and effective engagement. “The military hierarchy as I know is ready and willing to work with whoever has the nod. It’s how you relate to them, and give them that opportunity to perform their mandate per the Constitution.”

items.title: Tension à la BCRG : le syndicat menace de paralyser l’institution et accuse…
items.description: Le climat social se tend à la Banque centrale de la République de Guinée (BCRG). La délégation syndicale de l’institution, affiliée à l’Union syndicale des travailleurs de Guinée (USTG) et à la Fédération syndicale autonome des banques et assurances de Guinée (FESABAG), a annoncé ce vendredi 7 août 2026 le dépôt d’un préavis de grève, tout en dénonçant l’attitude des autorités actuelles de la BCRG. Lors d’un point de presse tenu à Conakry, les représentants des travailleurs ont confirmé avoir transmis, le jeudi 6 août, un préavis de grève à la direction générale de la BCRG. Le mouvement annoncé couvre la période du lundi 10 au jeudi 20 août 2026. À défaut d’un accord durant cette période, le syndicat menace de déclencher une grève générale illimitée jusqu’à la signature du protocole d’accord 2026. Selon le secrétaire général adjoint de la délégation syndicale, Aboubacar Sidiki Camara, ‘ ’cette décision fait suite au refus présumé du gouverneur de signer un protocole d’accord issu des négociations engagées autour de neuf points de revendication .’’ « Nous avons mené plusieurs démarches qui n’ont pas abouti. Les autorités refusent d’exécuter le protocole d’accord de 2026. Nous avions formulé des préalables prioritaires, notamment la prise en charge des évacuations sanitaires des employés. Malgré la validation de trois dossiers de malades, aucune suite n’a été donnée. Certains collègues sont décédés, d’autres sont devenus invalides. Nos camarades en détachement ont également été abandonnés », a déclaré le responsable syndical. Les travailleurs dénoncent également ce qu’ils qualifient de « blocages » dans le processus de négociation. « Un accord de principe avait pourtant été trouvé et un projet de protocole rédigé. Mais la signature a été retardée par plusieurs manœuvres. Des informations sur les revenus des employés auraient ensuite été collectées et diffusées sur les réseaux sociaux, ce qui met en danger l’image et la crédibilité de l’institution », a ajouté Aboubacar Sidiki Camara. S’appuyant sur les dispositions des articles 431.3 et suivants du Code du travail guinéen, la délégation syndicale indique avoir transmis une copie de sa notification à la FESABAG ainsi qu’à l’Inspection générale du travail (IGT). Elle appelle toutefois la direction de la BCRG à privilégier le dialogue afin d’éviter une escalade du conflit. « Nous invitons le cabinet à prendre les dispositions nécessaires pour trouver une issue favorable et constructive à cette situation et éviter un durcissement du mouvement syndical », a lancé le syndicat. Si aucun compromis n’est trouvé avant le 20 août, une paralysie de la Banque centrale pourrait avoir des conséquences importantes sur le fonctionnement du secteur bancaire et financier guinéen.

items.title: NELFUND disburses N303bn in student loans, urges North Central students to key in
items.description: By Edwin Philip, Lafia The Managing Director of the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND), Dr Akintunde Sawyerr, has said that 850,000 individual Nigerians have benefited from President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s student loan scheme, with more than one million loan applications received and N303 billion disbursed within two years. The NELFUND managing director disclosed this on Friday at the Federal University of Lafia, Nasarawa State, during the Renewed Hope Students Leaders Engagement and Digital Acceleration Programme for the North Central Zone. Addressing participants, Sawyerr explained that President Bola Ahmed Tinubu had, for the first time in the history of the country, taken the financial burden of education off the shoulders of parents and students by ensuring that nobody misses the opportunity to acquire education because of lack of funds or sponsors. He said, “The President has recognised this and he said we cannot let young people just be roaming around the street for any reason, not because they don’t want to learn, but because they don’t have money or they don’t come from rich homes. The President said that is not acceptable.” He added: “He has deployed this programme known as NELFUND to ensure that if you want to get an education and harness your potential to be a great citizen, you must not be prevented from getting that opportunity simply because you come from a poor home.” The NELFUND boss charged students from the North Central region to key into the programme, stressing that applicants do not need to know anybody to access the loan, as all the information required to apply is available online. “The President has made money available. Just make sure you are qualified for it. The system he has allowed us to put in place is digital-based. If you want to get this loan, you don’t need to know anybody. It doesn’t matter who I am; you don’t need to know me, you don’t need to have my number, you don’t need to connect to me. “You go online and put in specific pieces of information that confirm that you qualify. “Your name, your BVN, your matriculation number, your JAMB registration number and date of birth. Make sure you are in a school that is approved, a government tertiary institution,” he said. He, however, appreciated the Senior Special Assistant to the President on Student Engagement, Comrade Asefon Sunday, for working tirelessly to drive the process and serve as a bridge between students and the government by ensuring that the mandate of NELFUND is achieved. On his part, the Minister of Education, Dr Maruf Tunji Alausa, represented by the Director of University Education, Federal Ministry of Education, Dr Kareem Olawale Lateef, said the student loan scheme reflected the administration’s commitment to investing in Nigerian students and preparing them for leadership, innovation, entrepreneurship and the digital economy. “The Renewed Hope Agenda recognises that the future of our nation depends on the quality, capacity and resilience of its young people. As a student, you are not only a leader of tomorrow, but an active partner in nation-building,” he said. In his address, the Senior Special Assistant to the President on Student Engagement, Comrade Asefon Sunday, charged student leaders to promote excellence, uphold integrity, encourage dialogue, and foster peace and coexistence within their institutions and communities. He pledged his continued commitment to engaging Nigerian students, listening to their aspirations and creating platforms that empower them academically, economically and socially. “President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has achieved a lot; he has done a lot for Nigerian students. As young people of this country who are leaders of today, we no longer call ourselves leaders of tomorrow. Enough is enough. Today, our universities and tertiary institutions are now celebrating three years of uninterrupted academic calendars because of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu,” he said. Speaking earlier, the Vice Chancellor of the Federal University of Lafia, Prof. Muhammed Isa Kida, said the event affirmed the government’s commitment to student development and engagement. He commended the students for their discipline and dedication, charging them not to indulge in practices and lifestyles that could undermine the efforts of the government to make them responsible citizens and future leaders. Participants were drawn from tertiary institutions across the North Central Zone of Nigeria. The post NELFUND disburses N303bn in student loans, urges North Central students to key in appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: GPHA announces urgent measures to ease congestion at Tema Port
items.description: The Ghana Ports and Harbours Authority (GPHA) has announced a series of urgent operational measures to address growing landside congestion at the Port of Tema, assuring stakeholders that efforts are underway to restore normal cargo flow and maintain efficient port operations. According to the Authority, the congestion has been driven largely by a significant increase in import volumes, a corresponding rise in exports of empty containers, and increasing road traffic challenges around the port enclave. GPHA noted that similar congestion related challenges are being experienced at several ports across the West African sub region, resulting in delays in container evacuations and the movement of both laden and empty containers. In response, the Authority said it has activated enhanced operational interventions and placed all relevant stakeholders on heightened operational alert. The measures are being implemented in close collaboration with shipping lines and terminal operators to improve cargo movement and maximise available terminal capacity. Among the key interventions are efforts to accelerate the evacuation of empty containers through increased vessel calls, strengthen container transfer operations, deploy additional trucks, improve the handling and storage of empty containers, and optimise yard and traffic management systems within the port. The Authority emphasised that these measures are designed to reduce congestion, improve efficiency, and ensure the uninterrupted flow of international trade through Ghana’s largest seaport. GPHA has also appealed to importers, clearing agents, and cargo owners to expedite the clearance and evacuation of their consignments from the port. The Authority stressed that the prompt removal of cargo is critical to creating additional space within terminals, enhancing operational efficiency, and facilitating the smooth movement of goods. “Prompt cargo evacuation remains essential to easing pressure on terminal space and supporting the continuous flow of trade through the port,” the Authority said. GPHA further assured stakeholders that it is closely monitoring developments and will continue to implement the necessary interventions to address the situation and restore normal operating conditions as quickly as possible. The Authority expressed appreciation to the trading community and the general public for their patience, cooperation, and understanding during the period of congestion. GPHA reiterated its commitment to maintaining a safe, efficient, and competitive port system capable of supporting Ghana’s international trade ambitions and broader economic growth objectives.

items.title: Tinubu tasks WEC Nigeria on global energy leadership
items.description: By Obas Esiedesa, Abuja President Bola Tinubu has tasked the newly inaugurated World Energy Council (WEC) Nigeria leadership with positioning the country as a leading voice in global energy affairs and ensuring that Africa’s perspectives shape international energy decisions. Tinubu gave the charge while welcoming Nigeria’s formal admission as the newest National Member Committee of the WEC, describing the development as a proud moment for the country and a strong vote of confidence in its energy reforms and leadership role in Africa. The President, in a statement issued on Friday by his Special Adviser on Information and Strategy, Bayo Onanuga, said Nigeria’s entry into the century-old global energy network of more than 100 countries would enable the country to play a more active role in shaping global discussions on energy security, equity and sustainability. “Nigeria has joined the World Energy Council to lead, not just participate – to ensure Africa’s voice shapes global energy decisions,” Tinubu said. Nigeria’s return to the WEC comes with a newly constituted National Member Committee and Governing Board, with the Nigerian chapter expected to strengthen the country’s engagement in global energy policymaking and help attract investment for energy transition and industrial development. The WEC Nigeria platform is designed as an independent, impartial and technology-neutral forum bringing together government, industry, financial institutions, academia and civil society to address the country’s energy priorities. Its work will focus on Nigeria’s Energy Trilemma of energy security, energy access and environmental sustainability, while supporting efforts to expand electricity access, strengthen energy security, accelerate gas development and mobilise investment for sustainable economic growth. The Council said Nigeria’s membership would also connect local businesses and institutions to international knowledge, technologies, partnerships and investment opportunities through its network of more than 3,000 member organisations across over 100 countries. Tinubu congratulated the inaugural leadership of WEC Nigeria, led by Abdulrazaq Isa as Chairman and Bala Wunti as Chief Executive Officer, as well as members of the inaugural Board drawn from across the energy value chain, regulatory institutions, industry associations, finance, academia and the Future Energy Leaders community. The President described Isa as a distinguished patriot and industrialist whose investments in indigenous refining and industrial energy had opened a new frontier for Nigerian enterprise. He described Wunti as an energy strategist and reform advocate whose more than three decades of service had been marked by reforms aimed at strengthening national revenues and investor confidence in the energy sector. Tinubu said the combination of industry leaders, regulators, finance experts and youth leaders on the Board would provide the balance, neutrality and credibility required for WEC Nigeria to succeed. He affirmed the full support of the Federal Government for WEC Nigeria as a neutral, technology-agnostic platform for policy dialogue, investment mobilisation and innovation. The President also reiterated Nigeria’s commitment to working with WEC London and its global community to deliver secure, affordable and sustainable energy for all. He wished the Chairman, CEO and members of the inaugural Board success in what he described as a historic national assignment. The post Tinubu tasks WEC Nigeria on global energy leadership appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Rethinking assessment, achievement and ranking in Ghanaian education
items.description: WHEN THE RULER BECOMES THE RACE Rethinking Assessment, Achievement and Ranking in Ghanaian Education A Nunyãdume Reflection on What Our Examinations Should Actually Measure The Elders of Nunyãdume tell of a teacher who gathered ten children beneath the village tree and taught them to climb. At the end of the year, nine could climb the tree. The villagers celebrated. But the examiner shook his head. “ If nine have reached the top, ” he asked, “ how shall I know which child is first? “ So he measured how quickly each child climbed. One reached the top first. Another came second. Someone necessarily came ninth. And the tenth did not reach the top at all. The examiner proudly announced that he had successfully ranked the children. An Elder sitting nearby asked: “ But was our purpose to discover who could climb, or merely who climbed faster than another? “ The village became quiet. That question, I believe, deserves to be asked about Ghanaian education. What is the purpose of education? Education must certainly identify excellence. Universities and competitive programmes must select among applicants. Scholarships must sometimes distinguish among candidates. Schools with fewer places than applicants require mechanisms for selection. Ranking therefore has a legitimate place in education. But ranking is not education . And ranking is not the same thing as measuring learning. There is a fundamental distinction between the two questions: Has this child achieved the educational standard we established? and How did this child perform compared with other children? The first measures achievement . The second establishes relative position . Both questions can be legitimate. But they are not the same question. Our difficulty begins when we ask one examination grade to answer both. The BECE Paradox WAEC states explicitly that BECE candidates are graded using the stanine ( STA ndard NINE ), a method of scaling test scores on a nine-point standard scale with a mean of 5 and a standard deviation of 2. The earliest known use of stanine was by the U.S. Army Air Forces in 1942. More importantly, WAEC explains why: the system was considered appropriate for the dual purposes of certification and selection . WAEC further explains that stanine grading ranks and compares candidates’ performances relative to one another. Indeed, WAEC has explained that BECE does not operate with fixed grade boundaries in the ordinary sense; boundaries may vary according to candidate performance. There is nothing psychometrically illegitimate about norm-referenced assessment. The question is whether we are asking it to perform a task for which a different form of assessment may be more appropriate. Ghana’s curriculum philosophy increasingly emphasises competencies and performance standards . Our National Pre-Tertiary Education Curriculum Framework describes assessment as determining how far a learner has attained necessary knowledge, skills, attitudes and behaviours, and emphasises that, assessment should provide meaningful feedback about progress toward defined performance indicators. This presents us with an intellectually important question: If our curriculum is increasingly standards- and competency-oriented, should our principal assessment philosophy not also tell us whether those standards and competencies have actually been achieved? The Difference Between Achievement and Ranking Imagine that Ghana decides that every child completing JHS should be able to solve a particular level of mathematical problem. We invest in teachers. We improve textbooks. We introduce technology. We support struggling pupils. And eventually 90 per cent of our children master that competency. That should constitute a national educational triumph. A criterion-referenced assessment can tell us: Nine out of every ten Ghanaian children have attained the required mathematical competency. A norm-referenced system asks a different question: Which children performed better than the others? Even in an outstanding cohort, somebody remains at the bottom. Conversely, if an entire cohort performs badly, relative ranking can still identify its highest performers. That information is useful for selection . It is considerably less useful for determining whether Ghana’s educational system is actually succeeding. The distinction is fundamental: A nation should measure its children principally against what it promised to teach them, not merely against one another. The Mental-Health Question Why should the Chief Executive of the Mental Health Authority enter a discussion about educational assessment? Because examinations do not merely produce grades. They produce experiences. They influence identity. They influence family expectations. They influence anxiety. They influence self-worth. And, for some young people, they appear to determine their entire future. A child can easily move psychologically from: “I performed poorly in an examination” to: “I am a failure.” Those statements are profoundly different. One describes an outcome. The other defines a human being. An educational system must be demanding. Standards matter. Excellence matters. Competition will sometimes be unavoidable. But unnecessary competition should never masquerade as educational measurement. Educational psychologists, psychiatrists, teachers and policymakers should therefore ask not whether examinations cause some anxiety, that is inevitable, but whether the architecture of assessment unnecessarily transforms learning into perpetual social comparison . What, then, should Ghana do? I propose neither the abolition of BECE nor the abandonment of ranking. I propose something more conceptually coherent: Separate Certification from Selection. Certification should answer: “What has the learner mastered?” At both BECE and WASSCE levels, Ghana should progressively establish clearly defined, criterion-referenced competency standards. A grade should communicate meaningful information such as: Advanced proficiency. Proficient. Developing proficiency. Basic attainment. Below expected standard. The boundaries should be anchored, as far as psychometrically feasible, to what candidates demonstrably know and can do. The nation could then meaningfully compare educational outcomes across years. If Mathematics proficiency rises from 45% to 75%, Ghana should be able to celebrate that achievement without requiring some predetermined proportion of children to occupy lower categories. Selection should answer: “Where does the learner rank when places are scarce?” Where 20,000 qualified children compete for 5,000 places, ranking becomes necessary. Use an appropriate standardised score, percentile, placement index or other psychometrically defensible mechanism for that particular purpose . But call it what it is: selection. Do not confuse it with mastery. Thus a learner could receive: Mathematics: Proficient and, where necessary for competitive placement: National/placement percentile: 78th One tells the family what the child knows. The other tells the system where that child stands in a competition for scarce places. BECE and WASSCE should share one assessment philosophy; not necessarily identical grades This is where I would modify the proposition that started this discussion. I would not insist that BECE and WASSCE must necessarily use identical grading symbols. Their purposes and developmental stages differ. I would insist on something more important: From basic education through senior high school, Ghana should have one intelligible philosophy: achievement is measured against defined educational standards; ranking is separately reported when selection requires it. That creates continuity without forcing artificial uniformity. The Two Princesses of Nunyãdume The Stammering Linguist of Nunyãdume tells of two young princesses whose educational journey did not follow the familiar road. When other children travelled the conventional path towards the BECE, these two were educated for a period within the compound of the Chief Linguist. There were no school bells to announce the beginning of lessons. There were no positions in class to tell them whether they were first, fifth or fiftieth. But there were books. There was discipline. There was curiosity. There were expectations. There were examinations of another kind, the daily expectation that what had been taught must be understood, questioned and applied. And eventually, when the princesses left the compound and entered the larger educational world, something interesting happened. The absence of a BECE certificate had not meant the absence of learning. They progressed. They competed. And eventually, both gained admission to study medicine in Ghana. If Odomankoma , the Creator, grants them life and good health, they may in the coming years emerge as young doctors serving their country. The Elders of Nunyãdume did not tell this story to argue that Ghanaian children should be homeschooled. Neither did they suggest that two princesses constitute scientific evidence. Two children cannot establish national educational policy. Nor should an educational opportunity available to one family automatically be assumed feasible, appropriate or equitable for millions of Ghanaian families. The Elders told the story because it forced Nunyãdume to confront a more fundamental question: Is passing through every conventional examination necessarily synonymous with learning? The experience of the two princesses suggests that the answer cannot simply be yes . For an examination is an instrument for measuring education . It is not education itself. A weighing scale can tell the farmer something about his harvest. But the scale did not grow the maize. Likewise, an examination can tell us something important about what a child has learned. But sitting an examination did not, by itself, produce the learning. And ranking children tells us something else again. It tells us how one child performed relative to another . It does not necessarily tell us whether either child has attained the standard Ghana expected them to achieve. That distinction is fundamental. The Elders therefore asked: “If ten children reach the top of the tree, does the fact that one arrived tenth mean that child cannot climb?” Surely NOT . And if none of the ten reaches the top, does declaring one of them first mean that the village has successfully taught its children to climb? Surely NOT . Therein lies the distinction between achievement and ranking . Our educational system must first determine whether the learner has acquired the knowledge, competencies and intellectual tools we promised to teach. Where opportunities are scarce and selection becomes necessary, we may then ask who performed better than whom. But we should never confuse the second question with the first. For the ultimate purpose of education cannot simply be to determine which child stands above another . It must be to enable every child to stand . And perhaps that is the lesson the two princesses unknowingly taught Nunyãdume: There may be many roads to learning, but every road must eventually be judged by what the traveller knows, understands and can do, not merely by whether the traveller passed the same milestone as everyone else. The role of educational psychologists I believe Ghana’s educational psychologists should occupy the intellectual centre of this conversation. This should not become a political contest between those “for” and “against” WAEC. WAEC performs an indispensable national and regional function. Nor should politicians alone determine the answer. This is fundamentally a question of psychometrics, developmental psychology, pedagogy, curriculum design, equity, and public policy. Educational psychologists should help Ghana determine: What exactly does each examination purport to measure? Are grades valid measures of those constructs? What competencies constitute satisfactory attainment? How should standards be set? How stable should those standards remain across cohorts? When is norm-referencing appropriate? When is criterion-referencing preferable? What is the psychological effect of high-stakes ranking? How do socioeconomic inequalities influence apparent merit? How should school-based assessment complement external examinations? And how can assessment produce information that improves teaching rather than merely sorting children? NaCCA’s own mandate includes developing national curriculum and assessment standards and reviewing national assessments, making such a multidisciplinary reconsideration institutionally compatible with Ghana’s existing educational architecture. From examination system to learning system The Elders of Nunyãdume say: “When the farmer weighs his harvest, the scale does not make the maize grow.” Examinations are scales. They are important. They tell us something about the harvest. But weighing children more frequently does not educate them. Ranking them more precisely does not necessarily make them more competent. Our real national questions are harder: Can they read with understanding? Can they reason mathematically? Can they interrogate evidence? Can they communicate? Can they collaborate? Can they create? Can they solve unfamiliar problems? Can they disagree without becoming enemies? Can they use knowledge ethically? Can they continue learning after the examiner has left the room? If the answer is yes, education has succeeded, even if another child happens to be better. If the answer is no, a Grade 1 cannot rescue the system. A National Assessment Compact I would therefore propose that Ghana convene a technically led National Assessment Compact , bringing together NaCCA, WAEC, GES, the Ministry of Education, universities, Colleges of Education, educational psychologists, psychometricians, teachers, parents, students, mental-health professionals, and employers. Its mandate should not begin with: “Should we abolish stanines?” That prematurely prescribes the answer. It should begin with: “What information should Ghana’s national examinations provide about every child, and for what purpose?” Only after answering that question should we choose the measurement instruments. That is how science should inform policy. The Child Is More Than the Rank The Elders of Nunyãdume return finally to those ten children beneath the baobab tree. The examiner had arranged them from first to tenth. Then the Elder asked the child who came ninth: “Can you climb?” The child answered: “Yes.” “Then why,” asked the Elder, “have we spent the whole afternoon discussing the eight children who climbed before you?” There lies the philosophical heart of the matter. Ranking tells us who came before whom. Assessment should first tell us who can climb. And education must ultimately teach every child to climb. Ghana should therefore pursue an assessment system rigorous enough to recognise excellence, sensitive enough to identify difficulty, fair enough to accommodate different pathways, and intelligent enough to distinguish achievement from competition . Let us measure our children against high standards. Let us identify exceptional achievement. Where scarce opportunities require ranking, let us rank transparently and scientifically. But let us never confuse a child’s position in a distribution with the measure of that child’s potential. For the Elders of Nunyãdume say: “The fact that one bird flies higher does not mean the others have forgotten how to fly.” Our educational system should tell every Ghanaian child: how well they have learned, what they can do, where they need help, and how they can improve. Only after that, where necessity demands it, should we ask who came first. That is the difference between an educational system designed principally to sort children and one designed to develop them. And Ghana must choose development.

items.title: ‘Do I look like someone who can be bullied?’ – Agalga dismisses doubts over possible Majority Leader role
items.description: Builsa North legislator, James Agalga, has brushed aside suggestions that he could be intimidated in a possible role as Majority Leader. He insisted that his years of parliamentary experience have adequately prepared him to lead the business of the House. The MP said his experience as a Ranking Member, Committee Chairman and long-serving legislator has equipped him with the leadership skills required to serve as Majority Leader. His remarks come in response to comments by former Defence Minister and Minority Leader Dominic Nitiwul, who questioned his leadership credentials. Mr Nitiwul argued that although Mr Agalga is among the longest-serving Members of Parliament, he had not previously occupied one of the House’s top leadership positions. Responding to the criticism, Mr Agalga said he was confident his performance would ultimately determine how Ghanaians assess his leadership. “I think that the end shall justify the means. Do I look like somebody who can be bullied?” he asked on Accra-based Citi FM on August 7. “We leave the rest for the people to judge when we settle down to work.” He rejected claims that he lacks leadership experience in Parliament, pointing to the various positions he has held over the years. “I want to assure you that I am not new to leadership in Parliament. I have been ranking member for eight solid years. I am currently the chairman of the Defence and Interior Committee. And so, to that extent, it cannot be said that I am new to leadership,” he said. Mr Agalga further argued that his long tenure in Parliament has earned him the respect of his colleagues, making suggestions that he could be bullied unfounded. “I am a full-term Member of Parliament. And so, I do not think that any colleague of mine in the House can bully me,” he said. He maintained that the true measure of his leadership would only become evident when Parliament resumes sitting and his stewardship is put to the test. “But like I said, the end shall justify the means,” he added.

items.title: The Genre That’s a Shortcut to Wisdom
items.description: This is an edition of the Books Briefing, our editors’ weekly guide to the best in books. Sign up for it here. “How are you on theory ?” my editor asked me earlier this week. I knew what he was talking about—not my pet hypotheses about, say, the existence of cryptids, but rather a group of 20th-century French philosophers. Yet I didn’t know much else beyond that. I was familiar with Michel Foucault, partly from college coursework but largely from a popular meme that features his most famous concept, the panopticon . I know about Roland Barthes and the death of the author. I know that Derrida, Lacan, and Deleuze are names that I should know. “Not good,” I told him. First, here are four new stories from The Atlantic’s Books section: Icarus in the faculty lounge Someone is mysteriously snapping up used books around the world. What if Freud was right? “Out Here,” a collection of poems by the Black Seed Writers Group I could read their works for myself, of course. I could pick up Foucault’s Discipline and Punish at any one of the college bookstores that serve four major universities in my city. But frankly—and I don’t think I’m alone in this—I’d rather not. My preference as a busy adult is to begin my approach to foundational, complicated ideas with the help of a particular kind of book: the intellectual biography. The structuralists would hate this. Lynn Steger Strong makes exactly that point in an Atlantic essay published this week about a new group biography of these thinkers. I may be oversimplifying their ideas (as Strong writes, any “smooth summary inevitably sacrifices complexity”), but in general, they disregarded biography as a source of useful information about art; Barthes, especially, rejected literary criticism that drew on an author’s life to unlock the meaning of their work. “There was only the text, over which the writer had little control,” Strong explains. “Even the self was ultimately an unstable text.” This makes a biography of the cohort feel almost sacreligious. Emily Eakin’s new book, The Frenchmen , focuses on these men’s personal lives to illuminate their earthshaking writings. After finishing it, Strong wonders: “How could biography not be important?” I agree. Important ideas don’t just come to Earth fully formed and then flow through their speakers; they’re influenced by the wider context in which they develop. Earlier this year, when I was curious about the life and work of Karl Marx, the first book I reached for wasn’t Capital . Instead, I read Francis Wheen’s 2000 biography of the man —yes, I learned, he did ask Frederich Engels for money immediately after Engels told him that his beloved partner, Mary, had died. And yes, he really did spend ages in the British Museum’s reading room trying to squeeze as much information as possible into Capital (which is not to say that he didn’t miss anything). The biography also reminded me that Marx did not invent socialism; he was building on an intellectual tradition that predated him by decades. I encourage readers to try this out for themselves. Back in 2022, Talya Zax recommended nine group biographies that explain not only the lives of their subjects but also how those individuals influenced other people and movements. Personally, I’m on to a new topic: I’m about five chapters into Kai Bird and Susan Goldmark’s forthcoming biography of Roy Cohn, American Scoundrel , and the world of 20th-century New York City—an environment that incubated hundreds of famous and influential leaders, including our current president—is unfolding before me. Illustration by The Atlantic * How Theory Took Over the World By Lynn Steger Strong The French writers of the postwar era argued that the author’s life is irrelevant. Emily Eakin’s lively new book proves them wrong. Read the full article. What to Read The Haçienda: How Not to Run a Club , by Peter Hook The Haçienda in Manchester was a catalyst of the U.K. acid house scene in the late ’80s, and a prophecy foretold: “The haçienda must be built,” the Situationist poet Ivan Chtcheglov wrote in 1953. Heeding these cryptic words some three decades later, the audacious (and well-read) impresario Tony Wilson opened the Haçienda together with the circle of post-punk musicians and designers involved with his label, Factory Records. Their attempt to decipher Chtcheglov’s mystical phrase lasted 15 years. Hook, the bassist for New Order, served as a kind of player-coach at the Haçienda, helping manage its madcap affairs while his band became the club’s cash cow. In this memoir of misbegotten business administration, Hook returns to the storied nights out that changed British culture even as they threatened to bankrupt him—and worse. Beset by gangs and guns, the Haçienda faltered in the ’90s despite clever-sounding schemes such as replacing the club’s security with the gangsters themselves. This is a scrapbook of utopian folly, yes, but also an insider’s look at what was, for a time, the wildest workplace on Earth. — Andrew Holter From our list: Five books about going out that are worth staying in for Out Next Week 📚 Sunrise , by Téa Obreht 📚 Days of Miracle and Wonder: Paul Simon and the Trials and Triumphs of Graceland , by Ashley Kahn 📚 Under the Falls , by Richard Russo Your Weekend Read Will Oliver / Bloomberg / Getty Do Not Paint Granite! By Dorothy Robyn History and aesthetics aside, Trump’s plan violates a key rule of building maintenance : Do not paint granite. Granite is a superior building facade that has been used for other distinctive structures in Washington, D.C., such as the Library of Congress and the Old Post Office. Left unpainted, granite requires little maintenance. Once granite is painted, however (and examples are rare), it requires extensive maintenance in perpetuity. Greg Werkheiser, a co-founder of Cultural Heritage Partners , a law firm representing the DC Preservation League (which is suing over the project), has warned that the EEOB could become the Golden Gate Bridge of federal buildings : As soon as painting is finished on one end, it will be time to begin again on the other. Read the full article. When you buy a book using a link in this newsletter, we receive a commission. Thank you for supporting The Atlantic . items.title: SNCFT | Perturbations sur le trafic ferroviaire
items.description: La Société nationale des chemins de fer tunisiens (SNCFT) annonce, ce vndredi 7 août 2026, une perturbation du trafic ferroviaire à l'entrée sud de Tunis. Le mouvement des trains est actuellement perturbé dans les deux sens entre les gares de Tunis et de Jbel Jelloud, impactant aussi bien la ligne des banlieues sud que les lignes de grandes distances, indique un communiqué de la SNCFT, ajoutant que la circulation s'effectue momentanément sur une voie unique. Cette situation est causée par deux facteurs simultanés : une panne électrique sur le câble de la deuxième voie et des travaux d'aménagement sur la troisième voie, menés dans le cadre du projet d'élargissement de l'entrée sud de la capitale. Tout en présentant ses excuses à sa clientèle pour la gêne occasionnée, la SNCFT précise que ses équipes techniques sont actuellement mobilisées sur le terrain pour effectuer les réparations nécessaires et rétablir la circulation normale dans les plus meilleurs délais. Y. N. L’article SNCFT | Perturbations sur le trafic ferroviaire est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: West Africa Champions Cup 2026 : neuf clubs ouest-africains attendus pour la 5ème édition
items.description: La 5e édition de la West Africa Champions Cup se déroulera du 14 au 22 août 2026 au stade M’Ballou Mady Diakité de Kankan. L’annonce a été faite ce vendredi 7 août par les organisateurs, à l’occasion d’une conférence de presse consacrée aux préparatifs de la compétition. Initialement annoncée avec la participation de dix clubs, cette édition réunira finalement neuf formations après le forfait de dernière minute du club soudanais d’Al Hilal SC. La Guinée sera représentée par trois clubs : le Horoya AC, le Hafia FC et le Karfamoriah FC. Le Mali, pays le plus représenté, alignera quatre équipes : le Djoliba AC, le Stade Malien, le Real de Bamako et le FC Diarra. La Sierra Leone sera présente avec Star Sport, tandis que la Mauritanie sera représentée par le FC NZidane. Créée il y a cinq ans, la West Africa Champions Cup vise principalement à offrir aux clubs de la sous-région une meilleure préparation avant le lancement des championnats nationaux et des compétitions interclubs de la CAF. Pour le promoteur de la compétition, Alpha Mady Touré, cette vision demeure le fondement du tournoi. « Le tournoi est né du constat selon lequel nos clubs avaient un déficit de préparation avant les compétitions interclubs de la CAF », a-t-il expliqué. Selon lui, l’engouement suscité par la compétition auprès des clubs confirme son utilité. Il cite notamment la participation régulière du Djoliba AC et du Stade Malien, qui ont fait de ce rendez-vous un élément important de leur préparation. « Le Stade Malien s’est préparé depuis trois ans dans cette compétition », a-t-il rappelé, tout en soulignant l’intérêt constant des clubs guinéens pour le tournoi. Cette 5e édition a néanmoins été confrontée à des difficultés financières et logistiques. Les organisateurs indiquent avoir reçu plusieurs demandes de participation, sans pouvoir toutes les satisfaire. « Nous avons eu énormément de sollicitations, mais avec les contraintes financières et logistiques, nous avons été obligés de nous limiter à neuf clubs », a précisé Alpha Mady Touré. Le co-promoteur Cellou Tâta Diallo a, pour sa part, insisté sur les défis liés à l’organisation, notamment la prise en charge des délégations étrangères. « Dieu sait combien il est compliqué de prendre en charge ne serait-ce qu’une seule équipe », a-t-il déclaré. Après plusieurs éditions organisées dans différentes localités, la West Africa Champions Cup revient pour la troisième fois à Kankan. Pour les promoteurs, ce choix traduit la volonté de contribuer à la promotion du football à l’intérieur du pays et de rapprocher les grandes compétitions sportives des populations. Présente à la conférence de presse, la Fédération Guinéenne de Football a salué l’initiative. Son secrétaire général, Ibrahima Blasco Barry, a estimé que ce tournoi constitue un cadre précieux pour renforcer la préparation des clubs et favoriser les échanges sportifs entre les pays de la sous-région. À l’approche du démarrage des compétitions interclubs de la CAF, cette nouvelle édition devrait ainsi permettre aux équipes participantes de peaufiner leurs automatismes, d’évaluer leur niveau et de se mesurer à des adversaires issus de différents championnats ouest-africains.

items.title: KNUST marks 75th anniversary with medical, one health outreach at Anwomaso
items.description: The Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology, Kumasi (KNUST) has reaffirmed its commitment to community service and public health through a comprehensive Medical and One Health Outreach organised by its College of Health Sciences as part of the University’s 75th Anniversary celebrations. Prof. Francis Kemausuor Dean of the Faculty of Mechanical and Chemical Engineering, speaking on behalf of the Vice-Chancellor, Professor Christian Agyare, said KNUST’s 75th anniversary was not only an opportunity to reflect on its achievements in teaching, research and innovation but also to demonstrate its enduring responsibility to society. “KNUST’s seventy-five-year journey has been defined not only by excellence in teaching, research and innovation, but also by a strong commitment to service,” he said, adding that, as a public university, KNUST has a duty to ensure its knowledge and expertise directly improve the well-being of communities. He described the outreach as “a practical demonstration of that responsibility,” noting that it brought together professionals and students from various health disciplines to deliver integrated healthcare services to surrounding communities. Prof. Kemausuor commended the College of Health Sciences, the planning committee and participating schools and departments for collaborating to organise the outreach, stressing that multidisciplinary collaboration is essential to addressing today’s complex health challenges. He also expressed appreciation to traditional authorities, market leaders, community members and development partners for supporting the initiative through logistical assistance, equipment and supplies. Prof. Kemausuor urged health professionals, students and volunteers to deliver services with professionalism, compassion and respect while protecting patient confidentiality and ensuring that participants requiring further care received appropriate referrals. He encouraged residents to take full advantage of the available services by asking questions, providing accurate health information and following medical advice after the screening exercises. He noted that health screening is most effective when followed by appropriate action and continued care. Professor Fred Stephen Sarfo, Provost of the College of Health Sciences. Professor Fred Stephen Sarfo, Provost of the College of Health Sciences, described the outreach as a practical expression of the University’s commitment to translating knowledge into meaningful community service. “Today is a very important day for the College of Health Sciences. We are gathered not simply to mark an anniversary, but to demonstrate what seventy-five years of KNUST should mean in practical terms: knowledge translated into service, professional expertise brought closer to the people, and stronger partnerships between the University and its neighbouring communities,” he stated. Prof. Sarfo said that while the College is dedicated to training health professionals, advancing research and improving health outcomes, those responsibilities must extend beyond lecture halls, laboratories and hospitals into the communities where people live and work. He said the choice of Anwomaso Market as the venue was deliberate because markets serve as important centres of economic and social activity, making healthcare services more accessible to surrounding communities. Prof. Sarfo also underscored the importance of teamwork among healthcare professionals, noting that effective healthcare delivery depends on collaboration among doctors, pharmacists, nurses, dentists, laboratory professionals, physiotherapists, optometrists, veterinary professionals, public health practitioners and students. “No single profession can meet all the health needs of a community,” he observed, adding that the outreach also provided students with valuable practical experience in interprofessional collaboration, communication and patient-centred care. Encouraging community members to participate actively, he advised residents to openly discuss their health concerns with healthcare providers and comply with referral recommendations where further assessment or treatment was required. Prof. Sarfo also stressed the importance of preventive healthcare, noting that many diseases can either be prevented or effectively managed through regular health checks, healthy lifestyles, appropriate medication use and early medical consultation. He expressed appreciation to the organising committee, faculty, students, volunteers, traditional leaders, assembly representatives, market leaders, community mobilisers and development partners whose contributions made the outreach possible. Calling on members of the outreach team to uphold the highest professional standards throughout the exercise, he urged them to safeguard patient dignity, confidentiality and safety while communicating clearly with participants. “The value of today’s programme will not be measured only by the number of people screened. It will also be measured by the quality of the interactions, the referrals completed, the knowledge shared and the trust strengthened between the College and the communities,” he said. He described the outreach as both a celebration of KNUST’s 75th anniversary and a reaffirmation of the College of Health Sciences’ commitment to remaining responsive to the healthcare needs of Ghanaians. Nana Akwasi Poku, Gyaasehene of Anwomaso, speaking on behalf of the Anwomasohene, Nana Osei Boah III, expressed appreciation to KNUST and the College of Health Sciences for bringing the outreach to the community, describing the initiative as a significant contribution to the health and well-being of residents. He thanked the University for “bringing healing, care and essential health services to the residents of this community,” noting that the outreach would benefit many people who might otherwise have limited access to such services. Nana Poku encouraged residents of Anwomaso and neighbouring communities to participate fully in the programme and take advantage of the free medical consultations, screening and health education being offered. He also expressed hope that the outreach would become a recurring initiative rather than a one-time event. “I hope that this will not be the only time such a programme is held here. We welcome more of these initiatives in the future to continue supporting the health and well-being of our people,” he said.

items.title: Majority leadership change ‘shocking’ – ACEPA’s boss
items.description: The Executive Director of the African Centre for Parliamentary Affairs (ACEPA), Dr Rasheed Draman, has described the anticipated change in Parliament’s Majority leadership as “shocking”, warning that frequent reshuffles involving senior parliamentary figures risk undermining the separation of powers and disrupting legislative business. Dr Draman made the remarks during an interview on Top Story on Joy FM, following the nomination of Majority Leader Mahama Ayariga as Minister-designate for Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs by President John Dramani Mahama. Mr Ayariga’s nomination is expected to pave the way for Builsa North Member of Parliament James Agalga to assume the role of Majority Leader, pending the completion of the necessary parliamentary processes. Reacting to the development, Dr Draman said the move reflects a longstanding constitutional and governance concern over the close relationship between the Executive and the Legislature. “I think for me, it is shocking and that speaks to the issues that we have been talking about over the years, separation of power and the divorce of legislature from the executive.” According to him, abrupt changes in parliamentary leadership have historically affected the work of Parliament, with some legislative initiatives losing momentum whenever key leaders are reassigned to the Executive. “I have been following our Parliament for many, many years, and I know some legislative issues have suffered in the past when we have had this sudden kind of reshuffles.” Dr Draman said leadership continuity is important to sustaining parliamentary reforms and ensuring that ongoing legislative work is not interrupted by changes arising from Cabinet appointments. Despite expressing concern over the transition, he said he was hopeful that the work initiated by Mr Ayariga as Majority Leader would be sustained under his successor. “That is how it came to me, but I hope what Majority Leader Mahama Ayariga has started and has been championing over close to almost two years now will continue under the new leadership.”

items.title: Kankan prête pour la 5ᵉ édition de la West Africa Champions Cup : les organisateurs font le point avec les médias
items.description: À quelques jours du lancement officiel de la cinquième édition de la West Africa Champions Cup (WAC) 2026 à Kankan, les organisateurs ont animé une conférence de presse ce vendredi 7 août 2026 afin de présenter les grandes articulations de cette compétition qui réunit neuf clubs de la sous-région. Cette rencontre avec les médias a été marquée par les interventions des promoteurs Alpha Mady Touré et Cellou Tata Diallo, qui ont mis en lumière les objectifs du tournoi, les innovations de cette édition ainsi que les dispositions prises pour garantir son bon déroulement. Dans son intervention, le co-promoteur du tournoi, Cellou Tata Diallo, a précisé : « La compétition va réunir neuf clubs. Au départ, il y en avait dix, mais les Soudanais d'Al Hilal se sont finalement retirés au dernier moment, arguant du fait qu'il y a une forte pluviométrie en Guinée. Donc, ça ne permet pas d'avoir de bonnes conditions de préparation, même si on sait qu'à Kankan, il ne pleut pas trop. Donc, nous restons avec neuf clubs : les quatre clubs maliens, dont deux en Ligue des champions et deux en Coupe de la Confédération, un club sierra-léonais qui est en Ligue des champions, un club mauritanien, deux clubs guinéens, le Horoya et le Hafia, engagés respectivement en Ligue des champions et en Coupe de la Confédération, et puis il y a le Karfamoriah FC de Kankan, dont le président nous accompagne depuis plusieurs années. Au niveau des nouveautés, comme on l'a dit, c'est que la RTG accepte d'accompagner cette fois la compétition. On aura la possibilité, cette fois-ci, non pas de passer par Internet, mais de faire une diffusion par satellite. Donc, il y aura une réalisation multicaméra avec le ralenti et tout ce qu'il y a autour. L'autre nouveauté, c'est de garantir à chaque équipe trois matchs et puis, au bout, on verra les deux équipes les mieux classées jouer la finale. » Le secrétaire général de la Fédération Guinéenne de Football, Elhadj Ibrahima Blasco Barry, a salué cette initiative, qui contribue au développement du football ouest-africain et au renforcement des échanges entre les jeunes talents de la sous-région. « Permettez-moi, au nom de la Fédération Guinéenne de Football, de saluer cette belle initiative qui contribue au rayonnement du football guinéen et au renforcement de la coopération sportive entre les pays de notre sous-région. Je tiens à rendre un hommage appuyé aux promoteurs de cette compétition, Alpha Mady Touré et Cellou Tata Diallo, ainsi qu'à l'ensemble du comité d'organisation. Dans un contexte où les ressources sont souvent limitées, ils ont fait preuve d'une détermination remarquable, d'une résilience exemplaire et d'un engagement sans faille pour faire aboutir ce projet ambitieux », a déclaré le responsable de l'instance dirigeante du football guinéen. Présente à cette rencontre, la directrice générale de la Radio Télévision Guinéenne (RTG), Makeme Bamba, a réaffirmé l'engagement du média de service public, diffuseur officiel de cette 5ᵉ édition, à assurer une couverture médiatique de qualité afin de rapprocher les passionnés de football de cet événement majeur organisé à Kankan. À ce sujet, elle a déclaré : « Nous avons eu ce partenariat et nous avons dit : nous allons accompagner. Cet accompagnement va non seulement permettre le premier tournage avec ce nouveau car de reportage, mais aussi permettre à l'équipe de bien maîtriser les équipements qui se trouvent dans ce nouveau car afin de nous propulser et d'aller plus loin. Ne pas se contenter des matchs guinéens, mais aussi des matchs de la sous-région, pourquoi pas si le résultat est concluant. » Pendant neuf jours, du 14 au 22 août 2026, les passionnés de football vibreront au rythme des affiches opposant les neuf clubs engagés dans cette édition : Horoya AC, Hafia FC et Karfamoriah FC (Guinée), Stade Malien de Bamako, Djoliba AC, Réal de Bamako et FC Diarra (Mali), Star Sport Academy (Sierra Leone), ainsi que FC Zidan (Mauritanie), invité de prestige. Une compétition qui promet un spectacle de haut niveau et confirme l'ambition de la West Africa Champions Cup de s'imposer comme l'un des grands rendez-vous du football ouest-africain. items.title: KiDi sets August 27 for release of third album ‘Where Do We Go From Here’
items.description: Months after hinting at an upcoming album, it appears the coast is clear now for music superstar KiDi, to release his third studio album. The two-time TGMA Album of the Year winner has announced that his project ‘Where Do We Go From Here’ will finally be out on August 27, 2026, on all music stores. In a post sighted on his Instagram account, he wrote: “10 years of hits, memories, and timeless moments with you.” “Now the journey continues. My third studio album WHEREDOWEGOFROMHERE?#WDWGFH August 27th.” The post has been met with exciting reactions from fans who simply can’t wait to hear what KiDi has been working on for the last two years. In the coming days, the singer will reveal track titles on the album as well as regional and international features. Since 2024, the platinum artiste, promised his fans a third studio album after the successes of his previous projects which topped the charts and were adjudged ‘Album of the Year’. In 2020, his debut album ‘Sugar’ was voted the best at the 2020Ghana Music Awards. The sensational singer repeated the feat at the 2022 Telecel Ghana Music Awards with his sophomore project ‘The Golden Boy’. KiDi’s second album was truly gold. The masterpiece helped him win the coveted ‘Artiste of the Year’ at the 2022 Telecel Ghana Music Awards. As part of the rollout for ‘WDWGFH’, the music icon is expected to embark on a number of promotional activities, including a listening session in London and Accra as well as an album release party. KiDi will also stage his first-ever solo headline concert in the United Kingdom (UK) at ‘HERE at Outernet’ on September 24, where he will perform all tracks on ‘WDWGFH’ to a live audience.

items.title: Trafic de motos volées à Conakry : un vaste réseau démantelé et plusieurs engins saisis
items.description: Les services spéciaux ont présenté à la presse, ce vendredi, onze hommes soupçonnés d'appartenir à un réseau spécialisé dans le vol, le recel et la revente de motos à Conakry. L'opération, menée à Mafanko, sur la Route du Niger, a permis la saisie de plusieurs engins dont les caractéristiques auraient été volontairement modifiées afin d'en dissimuler l'origine. Selon le commissaire principal de police Foromo Soropogui, en service à la Direction de lutte contre le crime organisé, l'enquête a été ouverte à la suite d'informations fournies par des sources jugées crédibles et confirmées par plusieurs recoupements. Ces renseignements faisaient état de l'existence d'un réseau opérant à partir d'un garage où exerçaient notamment des mécaniciens et des électriciens. « À la suite de dénonciations provenant de sources crédibles, recoupées par plusieurs autres informations, notre service a procédé, le 4 août 2026, à l'interpellation de onze personnes et à la saisie de plusieurs motos volées », a déclaré le responsable policier. D'après les enquêteurs, les motos dérobées étaient rapidement acheminées vers ce garage où elles faisaient l'objet de multiples transformations. Les membres présumés du réseau remplaçaient notamment le réservoir, le phare ou encore la selle, modifiaient l'apparence générale des engins et falsifiaient les numéros de châssis afin de rendre leur identification quasiment impossible. Le commissaire Soropogui affirme également que le réseau se procurait de fausses clés, de faux certificats d'immatriculation ainsi que des plaques d'immatriculation grâce à la complicité présumée de certains agents, avant d'écouler les motos sur le marché. Les personnes interpellées, âgées de 27 à 44 ans, sont : Sékou Camara, présenté comme le chef présumé du réseau, Mamady Cissé, Sayon Kaba, Idrissa Condé, Souleymane Traoré, Alya Camara, Sory Doumbouya, Oumar Sory Savané, Mahamed Lamine Bangoura, Abdoulaye Traoré et Ibrahima « Ilaye » Condé. Au cours de leurs auditions, les mis en cause ont rejeté les accusations portées contre eux. La police soutient toutefois que les motos saisies ne disposaient d'aucun document administratif et que leurs numéros de châssis avaient été falsifiés, des éléments qu'elle considère comme des indices sérieux de leur provenance frauduleuse. Parmi les suspects, Souleymane Traoré nie toute implication dans ce réseau et affirme n'avoir exercé que son activité de mécanicien. « Je ne fais pas partie de ce réseau. Je suis mécanicien. Lorsque des clients me confient une moto pour une réparation ou pour remplacer une pièce, je fais simplement mon travail. Je ne connais rien de cette affaire. Je travaille à Mafanko et je n'exerce que mon métier », s'est-il défendu devant les journalistes. Les onze suspects sont poursuivis pour association de malfaiteurs et vol aggravé, des infractions prévues et réprimées par les articles 784 et 374 du Code pénal, selon la police. Aux dernières nouvelles, ils devaient être déférés devant le tribunal de première instance de Mafanco, où la justice devra établir les responsabilités de chacun dans cette affaire.

items.title: Kaloum – Deux mois de prison pour le vol de 11 barres de fer au port de Conakry : « C’est la première fois que je vole »
items.description: Chauffeur de profession, Naby Laye Moussa Camara a été condamné à deux mois de prison par le tribunal correctionnel de Kaloum, ce jeudi 6 août 2026, pour vol de onze (11) barres de fer au port autonome de Conakry. Le prévenu était poursuivi par le parquet pour avoir soustrait ces barres de fer dans l’enceinte du port autonome de Conakry. Il était détenu à la maison centrale de Conakry depuis le 3 août dernier. Interrogé à la barre sur les faits qui lui sont reprochés, Naby Laye Moussa Camara a plaidé coupable. « Je suis chauffeur de camion au port autonome de Conakry. Je ne suis pas habitué à voler, c’est ma première fois de faire ça. Je demande pardon », a déclaré le prévenu. Dans ses réquisitions, le ministère public a requis deux mois de prison ferme contre le prévenu. Statuant publiquement et contradictoirement, le tribunal a déclaré Naby Laye Moussa Camara coupable des faits qui lui sont reprochés et l’a condamné à deux mois de prison. items.title: Pop Culture Has Its Teeth in You
items.description: In their fledgling but fascinating career thus far, the director Jane Schoenbrun has been consumed by the pop culture that consumes us. They’ve already proved to be an urgent voice on the matter: Their first feature, the low-budget We’re All Going to the World’s Fair , focused on the allure of online “creepypastas” and weird YouTube rabbit holes that despondent teenagers might go down. The second, I Saw the TV Glow , examined the psychological fallout of two isolated adolescents obsessed with a cult television series. Schoenbrun’s newest movie, Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma , is similarly interested in nostalgia: It follows Kris (played by Hannah Einbinder), a queer filmmaker tasked with rebooting a gruesome slasher franchise from yesteryear called Camp Miasma . As she does so, the past and the cynical present blend into a transfixing dilution of Schoenbrun’s interests and fears about identity and self through the prism of mass media. Schoenbrun’s previous films were intensely melancholic affairs, and it’s immediately clear that Camp Miasma is having a bit more fun with the same themes. It jabs at Hollywood’s impulse toward rampant intellectualization—and corporatization—of the cinematic junk food of decades past. Kris, who has a minor Sundance hit under her belt, endeavors to create a “woke” and hip take on Camp Miasma without alienating its enduring fan base. A charmingly stylized early montage establishes the franchise as akin to many 1980s VHS cult classics, garishly mixing gore, nudity, and an eerie campfire vibe. The film’s many sequels yielded diminishing returns, and the series eventually stooped to wacky concepts à la Friday the 13th —the main monster, Little Death, who carries a spear and wears a mask shaped like a cubic air vent, traveled to Manhattan, then space, and so on. At her hotel, Kris watches the original film and eagerly takes notes; during a cheesy sex scene, she scribbles DESIRE in her notepad and underlines it forcefully. Yet Kris, despite her intent to take a cerebral approach, also comes at the project with a teen sensibility. Any movie nerd might recognize her behavior: When she stops off at a gas station on a work trip, she grabs fistfuls of candy and then lazily spins through the cheapo DVD rack, excitedly calling a friend when she finds a junky Camp Miasma installment for sale. The opportunity to visit the now-abandoned sleepaway camp where the first entry was shot is both useful to her as a director and delightful to her as a fan. [ Read: Make culture weird again ] The film mostly takes place there, and Kris spends a bizarre weekend with Billy Presley (Gillian Anderson), a reclusive actor who starred in the original Camp Miasma but refused to participate in any of its follow-ups. Billy, however, now lives at the campground with the goal of giving herself what appears to be a peculiar form of exposure therapy. Anderson, herself a towering legend of genre television and cinema, is an imperiously fun and sexy figure for Einbinder’s nervous and dorky character to bounce off of. Billy seems both enticed and exhausted by Kris, who professes her struggle to bring an academic eye to the world of Camp Miasma . Billy reminds her that the franchise’s initial appeal was straightforward: The draw was “flesh and fluids.” As Kris spends more time with Billy, Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma metamorphoses from an industry satire into a dreamlike reflection on how what we watch can shape us, no matter how lowbrow. Schoenbrun renders the desolate grounds with beautiful matte-painted backgrounds; as Kris and Billy watch the old film, the fuzzy visuals and synthy score bleed away into contemporary CGI blood and carnage. Both the throwback and present-day imagery look surreal; even though Kris can identify the obvious tropes in Camp Miasma , she can’t seem to face the power that familiar scripts hold over her. And in a fantastical twist, Little Death somehow finds its way out of the Camp Miasma movies, emerging from the on-site lake. But this is not a tale of cinema coming to life and invading the mundane real world; it’s more about two different styles of storytelling blending into one. As past and present, “fiction” and “reality” swirl together for an inscrutable final act, Schoenbrun finds a fresh way to make an incisive observation about 21st-century life: Today’s moviegoers are immersed in their screens and hungry for pop culture, to the point that a trashy flick such as Camp Miasma can feel intrinsic to Kris’s sense of self. Someone like Kris may want to interrogate that relationship over and over in search of meaning, but perhaps it’s best not to subject what we watch to endless analysis and meta-critique. Instead, we may be better off embracing how we feel.

items.title: Africa Golf Tourism Convention 2026 reveals speakers for inaugural Ekurhuleni gathering in South Africa
items.description: Organisers of the inaugural Africa Golf Tourism Convention (AGTC) 2026 have unveiled the first batch of speakers expected to headline the landmark event scheduled for Ekurhuleni, Gauteng, South Africa. The four-day convention, set for August 18 to 21, 2026, aims to create a unified marketplace connecting Africa’s golf, tourism, hospitality and trade sectors while positioning the continent as a competitive destination for high-value sports tourism. The speaker line-up brings together senior public officials, tourism executives, hospitality professionals, business leaders and sports personalities from across Africa and beyond. Among those confirmed are Acting Chief Executive Officer of the Gauteng Tourism Authority, Crezelda Venter; Chief Destination Marketing Evangelist at Visit Gauteng, Barba Gaoganediwe; Head of the Gauteng Convention & Event Bureau, Nonnie Kubeka; and Global President of Circle of Global Business Women, Dr Sindiswa Mzamo. The convention will also feature commercial and international voices including Peter Tshidi, Director of Medium and Small Properties at Sun International; António Louro, Executive Director of Mangais Golf Resort in Angola; Joaquin Valverde, General Manager of the Spanish Chamber of Commerce South Africa; and Sadiq Dindar, Founder of AfriLuxe Tourism Advisory Services. Other speakers include Gauteng Tour Operators Association President Victor Sibeko, Founder and President of the Chamber of Business and Tourism Dr Tebogo Mokope Modjadji, television sports presenter OG Molefe, golf lifestyle entrepreneur Innocentia Motau and wellness advocate Sonia Booth. Founder and Convention Director of AGTC, Neo Peete, said the selected speakers reflect the convention’s ambition to provide strategic insights into Africa’s tourism and hospitality landscape. “Our objective from inception was to assemble a faculty of genuine change-makers who possess deep operational and strategic insights into Africa’s tourism, trade and hospitality dynamics,” she said. Neo Peete added that the event would provide delegates and exhibitors with practical approaches to developing sports tourism assets, expanding cross-border trade and creating new commercial opportunities. Co-founder and Exhibitions Director of AGTC, Gisele Masengo, said the convention provides a platform for tourism operators and golf-related businesses to connect directly with international buyers. “Africa represents one of the most promising frontiers for luxury sports travel, yet sellers of golf and tourism products have lacked a dedicated platform to present their offerings directly to qualified buyers,” she said. She encouraged destination management companies, hotel groups, golf resorts and sports apparel brands to register for exhibition spaces and trade passes. The first three days of AGTC 2026 will feature keynote sessions, business-to-business meetings, destination showcases, exhibitions and networking engagements involving tourism authorities, airlines, investors, golf industry leaders and international media. The convention will conclude with a championship golf day at Serengeti Estate, one of South Africa’s leading golfing destinations, where delegates will experience the link between golf, hospitality and business tourism. Organisers say the event is expected to strengthen Africa’s participation in the global golf tourism economy while creating new partnerships across the continent’s travel and leisure sectors.

items.title: Le CLO Doufelgou évalue la campagne de distribution de moustiquaires
items.description: Niamtougou, 7 août (ATOP) – Le Comité local d’organisation (CLO) de la campagne de distribution gratuite de Moustiquaires imprégnées d’insecticide (MII) du district sanitaire de Doufelgou a tenu, le vendredi 7 août à Niamtougou, une réunion d’évaluation post-distribution. Cette rencontre a permis de faire le bilan des opérations et d’apprécier les résultats obtenus. Elle a servi également de cadre pour identifier les difficultés rencontrées sur le terrain et de définir des stratégies destinées à renforcer la sensibilisation des populations en vue d’une utilisation régulière et correcte des moustiquaires distribuées. Les participants ​Les échanges ont révélé que la campagne s’est déroulée de manière globalement satisfaisante grâce à la mobilisation des différents acteurs. Toutefois, quelques difficultés ont été signalées par les équipes de suivi. Il s’agit notamment de l’absence de certains ménages recensés sur les sites de distribution, de l’impossibilité pour les responsables de formations sanitaires de joindre plusieurs chefs de famille par téléphone. Pour faire face à ces contraintes, les membres du comité ont recommandé le renforcement du suivi de proximité ainsi que la poursuite des actions de sensibilisation et de communication communautaire afin d’encourager l’utilisation quotidienne et correcte des MII, moyen efficace de prévention du paludisme. La présentation des opérations Le directeur préfectoral de la Santé de Doufelgou, Dr Alassani Nourou, a rappelé que la possession d’une moustiquaire ne suffit pas à elle seule à prévenir le paludisme. Selon lui, seule son utilisation effective et quotidienne permet aux populations de se protéger. Il a indiqué que les équipes sanitaires intensifieront les activités de sensibilisation de proximité et les visites à domicile afin de s’assurer que les MII reçues sont effectivement installées et utilisées au-dessus des couchages. Le préfet de Doufelgou, Colonel Aziaba Ayi Sessi, président du CLO, a estimé que les difficultés relevées ne remettent pas en cause les résultats de la campagne. Il a invité les membres du comité à maintenir le contact avec les ménages absents afin d’organiser des séances de rattrapage pour leur permettre de retirer leurs moustiquaires. ATOP/SG/TAL/BA
